title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
summary: Draw a plant's Bode plot by hand, adding one factor at a time with the magnitude and phase asymptotes, and read the factored form back from the asymptotic Bode plot.
text: A plant in factored form is a product of factors. In dB, the magnitude of the product is the sum of the magnitudes, and in degrees, the phase is the sum of the phases. So the Bode plot of a plant is drawn by adding, one factor at a time, the asymptotes of each factor. This is the central skill of the unit: without it, the Bode plot is a curve with no explanation. All frequencies are in hertz, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\).

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: The asymptotes of each factor
summary: Draw a plant's Bode plot by hand, adding one factor at a time with the magnitude and phase asymptotes, and read the factored form back from the asymptotic Bode plot.
text: Factor Magnitude (asymptote) Phase (asymptote) Gain \(G_0\) level \(20\log_{10} G_0\), flat 0° Real pole, \(1/(1 + s/\omega_p)\) 0 dB up to \(f_p\), then −20 dB/dec 0° at \(f_p/10\), −90° at \(10\,f_p\) Real zero, \(1 + s/\omega_z\) 0 dB up to \(f_z\), then +20 dB/dec 0° at \(f_z/10\), +90° at \(10\,f_z\) Pole pair, \(f_0\) and \(Q\) 0 dB up to \(f_0\), then −40 dB/dec 0° at \(f_0/10\), −180° at \(10\,f_0\) Zero pair 0 dB up to \(f_0\), then +40 dB/dec 0° at \(f_0/10\), +180° at \(10\,f_0\) The phase line of each factor goes from 0° one decade below the corner to the full value one decade above it, on a logarithmic scale. It gives −45° at the corner of a real pole, and −90° at \(f_0\) for the pair. With a high \(Q\), the real phase turns almost entirely near \(f_0\), and the two-decade line is off there (Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q).

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: The recipe
summary: Draw a plant's Bode plot by hand, adding one factor at a time with the magnitude and phase asymptotes, and read the factored form back from the asymptotic Bode plot.
text: Write the plant in factored form and read \(G_0\), and the level \(20\log_{10} G_0\). List the corner frequencies in increasing order: \(f_p\) and \(f_z\) of each real factor, and \(f_0\) of each pair. Draw the low-frequency line, flat, at the level of \(G_0\). As you pass each corner, add the slope of that factor: −20 dB per decade for a real pole, +20 for a real zero, −40 for a pole pair. The slope of the curve is the sum of the slopes already passed. Draw the phase the same way: add the phase lines of the factors, each centred on its corner. Mark the error at the corner. For a real pole, the curve sits 3 dB below the asymptote; for a real zero, 3 dB above. For a pair, the curve sits \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above the asymptote: above if \(Q > 1\), below if \(Q < 1\). The 3 dB error comes from \(|1 + j| = \sqrt 2\): at the corner, the real factor is \(1/\sqrt 2\) or \(\sqrt 2\). The pair's error comes from \(G(j\omega_0) = -jQ\): at the corner, the asymptote is 0 dB and the real curve is \(Q\). Both are derived from the canonical form, not conventions.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Example: the buck's plant at 9 Ω
summary: Draw a plant's Bode plot by hand, adding one factor at a time with the magnitude and phase asymptotes, and read the factored form back from the asymptotic Bode plot.
text: The plant, in the factored form of the averaged model ( \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] ), has \(G_0 = 23.9\), or 27.6 dB; a pole pair at \(f_0 = 4.96\) kHz with \(Q = 7.1\); and the ESR zero at 677 kHz. The recipe gives: a flat level of 27.6 dB up to 4.96 kHz; a slope of −40 dB per decade at 4.96 kHz, with phase −180° (from 496 Hz to 49.6 kHz); a slope of −20 dB per decade from 677 kHz on, since the zero adds +20 dB per decade. The zero's phase, +90° from 67.7 kHz to 6.77 MHz, adds to the pair's −180°: the plant's phase is −90° in that range. Comparing the asymptote with the real curve: Frequency Asymptote (dB) Real curve (dB) Error (dB) 500 Hz 27.6 27.7 +0.1 4.96 kHz (f₀) 27.6 44.6 +17.0 50 kHz −12.6 −12.5 +0.1 500 kHz −52.6 −50.7 +1.9 The large error is all at the pair's corner, and it is \(20\log_{10} 7.1 = 17\) dB. With a high \(Q\), the asymptote shows the shape, and the height of the peak comes from \(Q\). The +1.9 dB error at 500 kHz is not the pair's: it comes from the ESR zero's corner, at 677 kHz, which at that frequency is \(|1 + j\,0.74| = 1.24\), or +1.9 dB. The buck's plant at 9 Ω: the dashed curve is the plant, and the other is the design's loop gain, which the next unit explains. Compare the real peak with the asymptote of −40 dB per decade.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Reading back: from the asymptote to the equation
summary: Draw a plant's Bode plot by hand, adding one factor at a time with the magnitude and phase asymptotes, and read the factored form back from the asymptotic Bode plot.
text: The recipe runs in reverse, and it is the direction the student must master: the flat level at low frequencies gives \(20\log_{10} G_0\); each change of slope marks a corner: −20 dB per decade, a real pole at that frequency; +20, a real zero; −40, a pole pair with \(f_0\) at that frequency; the \(Q\) of a pair comes from the real curve at \(f_0\): \(Q = 10^{(L(f_0) - 20\log_{10} G_0)/20}\), with \(L\) the real magnitude in dB. This formula is exact only if the other factors are 1 at \(f_0\) (in the buck, the ESR zero adds 0.0002 dB there). If the real curve is not marked and \(Q\) is high, read it from the peak: \(Q \approx 10^{\text{peak}/20}\), with an error of 3.3 % at \(Q = 2\), 0.5 % at \(Q = 5\) and 15 % at \(Q = 1\). The peak does not separate a complex pair from two coincident real poles, because neither has a peak. Exercise A magnitude asymptote sits at 20 dB up to 1 kHz; it falls 20 dB per decade from 1 kHz to 10 kHz; and it falls 40 dB per decade from 10 kHz on. Write \(G(s)\) in factored form, ignoring the phase. Exercise Predict, then check on the figure. Before you look at the buck's figure, calculate the real magnitude of the plant at \(f_0 = 4.96\) kHz. The asymptote gives 27.6 dB. What does the real curve give there? Back to the converter The buck's plant is the one the figure above draws: the LC pair and the ESR zero, with the numbers of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). The origin of \(G_0\), \(f_0\) and \(Q\) from the circuit is in From circuit to factored form (reinforcement), an optional reinforcement.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: Feedback and margins
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: On its own, the buck regulates poorly: a step in the duty makes the output overshoot by 80 % of the jump and ring for 1.7 ms (Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q), and the gain changes with the input and the load. Feedback measures the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty. One trip around the loop goes through the controller, the plant and the sensor: \[T(s) = \beta\,G_c(s)\,G_m\,G_{vd}(s)\] In this course's converters, the ADC reads the output voltage itself, and \(\beta = 1\).

title: Feedback and margins
heading: What the loop buys: the sensitivity
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: \[S(s) = \frac{1}{1 + T(s)}, \qquad \frac{T(s)}{1 + T(s)} = 1 - S(s)\] Where \(|T|\) is large, a disturbance at the output comes out divided by \(|1 + T|\), and the output follows the reference. Where \(|T|\) is small, \(S \approx 1\): the loop does not act. Near the crossover, \(|1 + T|\) can be less than 1, and the loop amplifies the disturbance. That is the price of bandwidth.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: Crossover and margins
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: Crossover frequency \(f_c\): where \(|T| = 1\), or 0 dB, with the magnitude falling. In order of magnitude, it is the loop's bandwidth. Phase margin (MF): \(180^\circ + \angle T\) at \(f_c\). Gain margin (MG): how far, in dB, \(|T|\) is from 1 where the phase passes −180°. Both measure the distance from \(T\) to the point \(-1\), where the loop oscillates by itself, and both read in a concrete way: the MF is the extra delay the loop tolerates, \(\Delta t = \mathrm{MF}/(360^\circ f_c)\), and the MG is the extra gain it tolerates.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: A delay is not a pole
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\] A pure delay, \(e^{-s t_d}\), has a magnitude of 1 and a phase that falls in a straight line with \(f\), without limit. A pole changes the magnitude, and its phase stops at −90°. The delay is not a × in the s-plane, but it eats more margin the higher the crossover. The buck's loop gain with the 2p2z: read the crossover, the phase margin and the gain margin, and move the crossover to watch the margins fall.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: In the converters
summary: Why close the loop, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says and what the phase and gain margins measure.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: In the buck, with the 2p2z, the loop crosses at 8 kHz with a MF of 41° and a MG of 13.9 dB (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). From the model, \(|T| = 7.7\) at 100 Hz: a disturbance at that frequency reaches the output divided by 7.9 (\(|S|\) = −17.9 dB). At 8 kHz, \(|S| = 1.42\) (+3 dB): there the loop amplifies. The worst point is 9.8 kHz, where \(T\) comes within 0.62 of the point \(-1\). Extra delay tolerated: \(41^\circ/(360^\circ \cdot 8\,\text{kHz}) = 14.2\) µs, about 2.8 periods at 200 kHz. The delay the loop already has, \((1 + D)T_s = 6.875\) µs, takes 19.8° at 8 kHz (Computation and PWM delay). Extra gain tolerated: 13.9 dB, or 4.95 times. What the 41° margin means for the load step, and why the rule of thumb for damping misses here, is in From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails. Exercise A communication interrupt starts delaying the duty's write by a whole period, 5 µs. What happens to the 2p2z's MF? How many more periods would the loop take before oscillating? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the phase and gain margins from the measured response. Back to the converter With these ideas, go back to Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, which shows the margins of the buck's four controllers, and to Computation and PWM delay, which counts where the firmware's delay comes from.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: First-order pole and zero
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The first-order factors are the blocks \(1 + s/\omega\) of the factored form. This note covers a real pole and a real zero, and how each reads on the Bode plot.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: The pole
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad |G(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_p)^2}}, \qquad \angle G(j\omega) = -\arctan\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}\] On the Bode plot, a pole is drawn with two lines, the asymptotes: the magnitude stays at 0 dB up to the pole frequency, \(f_p\), and then falls 20 dB per decade; the phase stays at 0° and then falls to −90°. The real curve departs from the asymptotes only near the corner: at \(f_p\), the magnitude is \(1/\sqrt 2\), or −3.01 dB. The asymptote gives 0 dB there: the error is 3 dB; one decade below or above, the error falls to 0.04 dB; the real phase is exactly −45° at \(f_p\). The phase line, which goes from 0° at \(f_p/10\) to −90° at \(10 f_p\), also gives −45° at the corner, so it is right there. At the edges it is off by 5.7°: the real phase is −5.7° at \(f_p/10\) and −84.3° at \(10 f_p\). −3 dB is not half At \(f_p\), the magnitude is \(0.707\). Half, \(0.5\), is −6 dB, and that happens at \(\sqrt 3\,f_p\). In time, the pole gives an exponential: the response to a unit step is \(y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau}\), with \(\tau = 1/\omega_p\). It reaches 63 % of the final value at \(\tau\), 95 % at \(3\tau\) and 98 % at \(4\tau\). The higher the pole, the faster the response. A real pole: drag it along the real axis and watch the pole frequency on the Bode plot and the time constant in the step.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: The zero
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The zero, \(1 + s/\omega_z\), is the mirror of the pole: the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade above \(f_z\), the phase leads up to +90°, and the corner is also the point of +45° and 3 dB above the asymptote. On its own, the zero is improper: the gain would grow without limit, and the step response would contain an impulse, because \(s\) is a derivative. In a circuit, every zero comes with poles that limit the high-frequency gain. Together with a pole, \((1 + s/\omega_z)/(1 + s/\omega_p)\), the pair is realisable. A real zero on its own: the figure adds a far pole, ten times further away, so that the step exists.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: In the converters
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The ESR zero is a real zero, and it is the only first-order factor in the buck's plant: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\] In the buck, with 47 µF and 5 mΩ, it sits at 677 kHz. It adds 0.7° of phase at 8 kHz and 8.4° at 100 kHz, half the switching frequency. In the boost, with 100 µF and 10 mΩ, it sits at 159 kHz. Exercise Predict, then check on the figure. In the pole figure, the pole starts at 1 kHz. What are the magnitude and the phase at 10 kHz? Check on the Bode plot. Exercise A Bode asymptote sits at 20 dB up to 2 kHz and then falls 20 dB per decade. Write \(G(s)\) in factored form, with its DC gain. Exercise Write the asymptote of \(G(s) = \dfrac{10}{1 + s/(2\pi \cdot 1\,\text{kHz})}\): its level and its slope. Then give the real magnitude at 10 kHz. In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): how to obtain poles and zeros from a measured frequency response. Back to the converter The ESR zero is this first-order zero: go back to The ESR zero, which applies it to the buck's plant.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: The phase margin says how far the loop is from oscillating (Feedback and margins). What the oscilloscope shows, though, is the step: how far it overshoots the target and for how long it rings. This note bridges the two, and shows in the buck where the bridge gives way.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: From margin to step
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: Near the crossover, many loops look like an integrator followed by a pole, \(T = \omega_n^2/[s\,(s + 2\zeta\omega_n)]\). This course's buck is not one of them, as shown below. Closed, this loop is exactly a second-order pair, and the phase margin depends only on the damping: \(\mathrm{MF} = \arctan\big(2\zeta/\sqrt{\sqrt{1 + 4\zeta^4} - 2\zeta^2}\big)\). \(\zeta\) \(Q\) MF MF/100 Overshoot 0.2 2.5 22.6° 0.23 53 % 0.4 1.25 43.1° 0.43 25 % 0.6 0.83 59.2° 0.59 9.5 % 0.7 0.71 65.2° 0.65 4.6 % 0.8 0.63 69.9° 0.70 1.5 % Hence the rule \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{MF}/100\), with MF in degrees. In the integrator-plus-pole loop, it is off by less than 10 % between 37° and 67.5° of margin and by less than 15 % at any margin up to 71°; the error vanishes at 57.4°. Below that, the rule promises a little more damping than there is; above, a little less. That range belongs to the model loop, not to any loop. With \(\zeta\), the overshoot follows from the pair's standard form; for the lossless pair, \(\zeta = 1/(2Q)\), and the table gives both: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad s_{1,2} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2Q} \pm j\,\omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4Q^2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2\zeta}\] A real loop has more poles. The pair near the crossover is dominant when the others are at least five times further from the \(j\omega\) axis (ten, to trust the numbers) and no zero sits near it: then the step rings near \(f_c\) with the table's overshoot. When a pole sits closer to the axis than the pair, it rules the slow response.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: In the converters
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: In the buck, with the 2p2z, the loop crosses at 8 kHz with a MF of 41° (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). Damping. Predict: with a MF of 41°, the rule gives \(\zeta \approx 0.41\), \(Q \approx 1.2\) and about 25 % overshoot. Check: the closed-loop model gives a pair at 7.2 kHz with \(\zeta = 0.31\) (\(Q \approx 1.6\), 35 % overshoot): the rule promises a third more damping than there is. In QSPICE, the 1 to 2 A load step drops the output to 8.59 V, and it swings back to 9.14 V (The 2p2z compensator): the swing back is 35 % of the dip, what \(\zeta \approx 0.31\) predicts. Why the rule misses here. It assumes two things, and the buck meets neither. First, that the loop near the crossover is an integrator followed by a pole; the buck's is the plant near −180°, plus the compensator's lead and the firmware's delay. Not even the table's exact formula gets it right: with 41.3°, it gives \(\zeta = 0.38\). Second, that the pair is dominant. Besides the pair, the buck's closed loop has a real pole near 470 Hz, closer to the \(j\omega\) axis than the pair: by the criterion above, the pair is not dominant. The rule still gives the order of magnitude of the ringing near \(f_c\), but not the number, and it says nothing about the slow pole. The rule does not see everything The buck's 2p2z leaves \(|T|\) slightly below 1 between 1 and 2.4 kHz, where its zeros are. The margin does not see that. From the model, without the ADC's quantization, a slow tail of a few millivolts (5 to 6 mV at its peak) is left after the ringing; it decays with a time constant of about 0.34 ms and stays above 1 mV until about 1 ms after the step. It is the real closed-loop pole near 470 Hz. In QSPICE, it is lost in the simulated output's fluctuation of tens of millivolts. In the reference step, the same pole is no detail: the step has no overshoot at all, and the output takes more than 1 ms to reach 5 V. In QSPICE, it is still 0.45 V above 5 V 600 µs after the ramp starts, and 0.14 V at 1 ms. Reference ramp from 9 to 5 V with the 2p2z: the slow descent is the 470 Hz pole. A 1 to 2 A load step with the aggressive design, MF of 16°: compare the ringing with the 2p2z's, in the oscilloscope. Exercise Predict, then check in the figure. The aggressive design has a MF of 16° at 18 kHz. Before looking at the step: by the rule, what are the estimated \(\zeta\), the pair's overshoot and the ringing's period? Back to the converter With these ideas, go back to The 2p2z compensator, where the QSPICE load step is, and to Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, which shows the margins of the buck's four controllers.

title: From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)
heading: From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)
summary: Optional reinforcement. How to go from the circuit to the factored form, normalising the denominator, and where G₀, f₀, Q and the zero of the buck's and the boost's plant come from.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: This note is an optional reinforcement. The \(G_{vd}\) formulas are already in the converter notes; here you see the method that produces them, for the student who wants the factoring from the inside. The trail does not depend on it. Frequencies in hertz, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\).

title: From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)
heading: The method
summary: Optional reinforcement. How to go from the circuit to the factored form, normalising the denominator, and where G₀, f₀, Q and the zero of the buck's and the boost's plant come from.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: Write the ratio between output and input as a divider of impedances, \(N(s)/D(s)\). Divide \(D(s)\) by its constant term \(d_0\): \(D(s) = d_0\,(1 + a_1 s + a_2 s^2)\). Read the pole pair: \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{a_2}\) and \(Q = \sqrt{a_2}/a_1\), because \(1/(Q\omega_0) = a_1\) and \(1/\omega_0^2 = a_2\). Read the zeros in \(N(s)\), and the DC gain, \(G_0 = N(0)/D(0)\). Check: \(G_0\) has to be the circuit's DC gain, and the high-frequency slope has to match the number of energy-storing elements.

title: From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)
heading: Buck: the divider with the ESR
summary: Optional reinforcement. How to go from the circuit to the factored form, normalising the denominator, and where G₀, f₀, Q and the zero of the buck's and the boost's plant come from.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: The impedance of the output branch is \(Z_p = R \parallel (R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + 1/sC)\), which equals \(R\,(1 + sR_{\mathrm{ESR}}C)/(1 + sC(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}))\). The output is \(V_{in}\,Z_p/(R_s + sL + Z_p)\), with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\). Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(1 + sC(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) and dividing by the constant term, we get \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{V_{in}R}{R + R_s}\cdot\frac{1 + sR_{\mathrm{ESR}}C}{1 + a_1 s + a_2 s^2}, \qquad a_2 = \frac{LC\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}{R + R_s}, \qquad a_1 = \frac{L + C\,[R\,(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + R_s R_{\mathrm{ESR}}]}{R + R_s}\] By step 3, \(\omega_0\) and \(Q\) are those of the exact LC resonance ( \[\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R + R_s}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R + R_s)}}{L + C\left[R\,(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + R_s R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] ). At 9 Ω, \(a_2 = 1.03\cdot 10^{-9}\) s² and \(a_1 = 4.54\) µs: \(f_0 = 4.96\) kHz and \(Q = 7.1\), the numbers of Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q. The zero of the numerator is \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = 1/(2\pi R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C) = 677\) kHz. Exercise With the same \(V_{in}\) and the same losses, but with a 4.5 Ω load, calculate \(G_0\) and compare it with the 9 Ω value.

title: From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)
heading: Boost: the averaged plant without losses
summary: Optional reinforcement. How to go from the circuit to the factored form, normalising the denominator, and where G₀, f₀, Q and the zero of the buck's and the boost's plant come from.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: In the boost's averaged model (The averaged switch model), with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\) and no losses and no ESR, the linearised inductor and capacitor equations give the denominator \(sL(1 + sRC) + D'^2 R\) and the numerator \(R\,(D'V - I\,sL)\). The average current is \(I = V/(RD')\), and the term \(-I\,sL\) is the right-half-plane zero. Normalising by the constant term, \(D'^2 R\): \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{V}{D'}\cdot\frac{1 - s/(2\pi f_z)}{1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2}, \qquad \omega_0 = \frac{D'}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad f_z = \frac{RD'^2}{2\pi L}, \qquad Q = D'R\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\] With 12 V to 48 V, \(D' = 0.25\), \(R = 48\) Ω, \(L = 33\) µH and \(C = 100\) µF, we get \(V/D' = 192\) (45.7 dB), \(f_0 = 693\) Hz, \(f_z = 14.5\) kHz and \(Q = 20.9\). Note that \(f_z/f_0 = D'R\sqrt{C/L} = Q\): without losses, the zero and the pair are in the ratio \(Q\). Losses change this picture. With 25 mΩ of resistance in series with the inductor and an ESR of 10 mΩ, the term \(R_l/L\) dominates the damping, and \(Q\) drops from 20.9 to 4.4; the zero drops from 14.5 to 14.1 kHz, and the DC gain goes to 190. The full plant with these losses is in Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost. Exercise Calculate \(f_z/f_0\) for the lossless boost plant above, and check that it gives \(Q\). Back to the converter With the factoring done by hand, reread the buck's plant and the boost's: \(G_0\), \(f_0\), \(Q\) and the zero, for each one.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: PI, phase lead and the type III
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: A compensator is made of the same first-order blocks as the plant, chosen to give the loop gain two things: high gain at low frequency and enough phase at the crossover.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: The integrator: zero steady-state error
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: With the loop closed, the steady-state error to a reference step is \(1/(1 + T(0))\). If the compensator is just a gain \(K\), \(T(0) = K\,G_{vd}(0)\) is finite, and some error always remains. In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) = 23.9\): for less than 1 % error, \(K\) would have to exceed 4, and the crossover would go where the phase leaves no margin. A pole at the origin, \(K_I/s\), makes \(T(0)\) infinite, and the error to a step goes to zero. The price is the integrator's phase, −90° at every frequency, which adds to the plant's.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: The PI: integrator plus a zero
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: \[G_c(s) = K_I\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{s}\] The zero gives phase back above \(\omega_z\): well above it, the PI behaves like a gain, with phase near 0°. With the zero a decade below the crossover, the integrator barely weighs on the margin. But the PI never gives positive phase, and the buck, above resonance, is already near −180°.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: Phase lead
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: \[G_c(s) = \frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\omega_p}{\omega_z} > 1, \qquad \sin\varphi_{\max} = \frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + 1}\] It is a zero followed by a higher pole. Between the two, the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade and the phase forms a hill, with the peak \(\varphi_{\max}\) at the geometric mean, \(\sqrt{\omega_z\,\omega_p}\). The peak is placed on the crossover. Lead has diminishing returns: \(\alpha\) 2 4 9 16 100 \(\varphi_{\max}\) 19.5° 36.9° 53.1° 61.9° 78.6° Each lead costs gain at high frequency, \(20\log_{10}\alpha\), which amplifies noise and ripple. For the same phase, two smaller leads always cost less gain than a single one, and the difference grows with the phase: 9.2 against 9.5 dB for 30°, 19.1 against 22.9 dB for 60°, 26.5 against 42.3 dB for 80°.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: The type III: integrator plus two leads
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: The analog type III compensator of a voltage-mode buck is an integrator with two leads, usually equal: \[G_c(s) = \frac{K_I}{s}\left(\frac{1 + s/\omega_0}{1 + s/\omega_p}\right)^2, \qquad K_I = K\,\omega_0\] The two zeros sit near the LC resonance, where the plant takes up to 180°, and give up to 180° of phase, minus what the poles take; the two poles limit the gain above the crossover. The buck's loop gain with the 2p2z: move the zeros and the pole and watch the phase margin; the gain is recomputed to keep the crossover.

title: PI, phase lead and the type III
heading: In the converters
summary: The integrator brings the steady-state error to zero and costs 90° of phase; phase lead gives phase back at the crossover; the type III is an integrator with two leads, and the 2p2z is its digital relative.
text: The buck's 2p2z has an integrator, two zeros at 2 kHz and one pole at 60 kHz: one high-frequency pole fewer than the type III. It reads as a PI times a lead: \[C(s) = K_I\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_{z1}}{s}\cdot\frac{1 + s/\omega_{z2}}{1 + s/\omega_p}\] At 8 kHz, the crossover, with the continuous prototype: the PI (integrator and zero at 2 kHz) gives \(-90^\circ + 76.0^\circ = -14.0^\circ\); the lead (zero at 2 kHz, pole at 60 kHz, \(\alpha = 30\)) gives \(+68.4^\circ\), close to its maximum of 69.3° at 11 kHz; the total is \(+54.3^\circ\). The plant with the delay is at −191°, and the loop ends at −137°. Discretised by matched poles and zeros, the compensator loses 2° (The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping), and the margin is 41°. With the PI alone, the loop's phase at 8 kHz would be \(-191^\circ - 14^\circ = -205^\circ\): no margin at all. It is the lead that pays the bill. Exercise Predict, then check in the figure. Move the 2p2z's zero 2 from 2 kHz to 8 kHz, onto the crossover. How much phase does that zero stop giving, and what should the new margin be? Exercise A colleague swaps the 2p2z for a PI with its zero at 2 kHz, keeps the crossover at 8 kHz, and the buck starts oscillating. Explain it with the phase. In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the type III compensator designed from the measured plant. Back to the converter The full design, the coefficients in \(z\) and the link to the PID are in The 2p2z compensator; what happens to the integrator when the duty saturates, in Anti-windup and duty saturation.

title: Right-half-plane zero
heading: Right-half-plane zero
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: So far the zeros sat left of the \(j\omega\) axis, at \(s = -\omega_z\). Flipping the sign, the zero moves to \(s = +\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), the right half-plane: \[G(s) = 1 - \frac{s}{\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}}}, \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = 2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}} > 0\] The minus sign puts the zero on the right; \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), in hertz, is the zero's frequency.

title: Right-half-plane zero
heading: The magnitude does not see the side; the phase does
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: At \(s = j2\pi f\), the magnitude is \(\sqrt{1 + (f/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})^2}\), the same as an ordinary zero's: it rises 20 dB per decade above \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\). The phase is \(-\arctan(f/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\): instead of leading up to +90°, it falls to −90°, like a pole's. A pole's phase, a zero's magnitude An ordinary pole and a right-half-plane zero both take 90° of phase. The difference is in the magnitude: the pole brings the gain down, the right-half-plane zero raises it. For the loop it is the worst combination: more gain and less phase at the same time.

title: Right-half-plane zero
heading: It is not an unstable pole
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: Stability depends only on the poles. A system with all its poles on the left and a zero on the right is stable: its step response settles. It is non-minimum phase: it has more phase lag than the function with the same magnitude and the zero mirrored to the left, the minimum-phase one. What the zero changes in time is the start. Right after the step, the output moves the opposite way to its final value, and only then turns around: this is the inverse initial response. Two poles and a zero at 2 kHz: the button mirrors the zero between the half-planes. The magnitude does not change; the phase and the step's start do.

title: Right-half-plane zero
heading: Why it limits the crossover
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: A compensator cancels an ordinary zero by putting a pole on top of it. To cancel a right-half-plane zero it would need a right-half-plane pole: an unstable controller. That is not done. What is left is to cross well below the zero, where its lag \(\arctan(f_c/f_z)\) is still small and phase margin is left. The rules of thumb range from \(f_c < f_z/3\), which costs 18.4°, to \(f_c < f_z/5\), which costs 11.3°, depending on the source and on whether the nominal zero or the worst-case one is used. When the compensator puts its zeros at \(f_0\), the resonance, and crosses above \(3f_0\), the window \(3f_0 < f_c < f_z/3\) exists only if \(f_z/f_0 > 9\); in the lossless boost, \(f_z/f_0\) is the pole pair's own \(Q\), and in the lab, at 10 V and 2 A, the window is empty.

title: Right-half-plane zero
heading: In the converters
summary: A zero right of the jω axis has an ordinary zero's magnitude and a pole's phase; it destabilises nothing, but makes the step start the wrong way and limits the crossover.
text: In the boost, raising the duty keeps the inductor disconnected from the output for longer; at the first instant the output receives less current and falls. That is where the zero comes from (the full physics is in The right-half-plane zero): \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{2\pi L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\] With the boost's averaged model, from 12 V to 48 V: Point \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) Phase taken at 1.5 kHz At 4 kHz Initial dip in a step of \(d\) 12 V, 1 A (48 Ω) 14.1 kHz 6.1° 15.8° 0.1 % 12 V, 2 A (24 Ω) 6.9 kHz 12.3° 30.2° 0.5 % 10 V, 2 A (24 Ω) 4.7 kHz 17.8° 40.6° 0.7 % The boost's 2p2z crosses at 1.5 kHz, where the zero takes 6.1° to 17.8°; at 12 V and 2 A, that is \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\), between the 1/5 and 1/3 rules; the aggressive design, at 4 kHz, loses its margin when the load doubles. Look at the dip: in the lab, the zero sits 8 to 20 times above the resonance, which lies between 570 and 690 Hz, and the plant's inverse response barely shows in the step, a fraction of 1 % for a few tens of microseconds. The zero's harm is not in the dip; it is in the phase it takes near the crossover. The boost's poles and zeros, from the averaged model, with the 1.5 kHz crossover marked. The lab's range is 12 V (10 V in the input step) and loads of 24 to 48 Ω; the controls go from 9 to 15 V and from 24 to 480 Ω. The controls go a little beyond what the lab simulates. At the worst end, 9 V and 24 Ω, the inductor current reaches 11 A, the zero falls to 3.7 kHz and the resonance to 511 Hz: the zero already takes 22° at 1.5 kHz, but the dip is still only 0.9 %. At the other end, 15 V and 480 Ω, the zero rises to 226 kHz, beyond the ESR zero, and takes almost no phase at the crossover. Exercise Predict, then check in the figure. In the first figure, the zero starts at +2 kHz, in the right half-plane. Before pressing the button that mirrors it to −2 kHz: what happens to the magnitude, to the phase at 2 kHz and to the start of the step? Exercise A boost rings after a 1 to 2 A load step. A colleague proposes raising the compensator's gain to "make it stiffer". What do you answer? title: Second-order filters: the catalogue
heading: Second-order filters: the catalogue
summary: The five second-order filters with a pole pair, each as a factored form with f₀ and Q, and the asymptote that identifies it on the Bode plot.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: Every second-order filter with a pair of poles uses the same denominator, \(1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2\), the one from the previous note. What changes from one filter to another is the numerator. The table gives each numerator, the low- and high-frequency asymptotes and what the real curve does at \(f_0\). All frequencies are in hertz, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Filter Form, with \(D(s) = 1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2\) Asymptote at low frequency Asymptote at high frequency Real value at \(f_0\) Low-pass \(G_0/D\) 0 dB, 0° −40 dB/dec, −180° \(Q\) (+20 log Q dB) High-pass \(G_0 (s/\omega_0)^2/D\) −40 dB/dec, +180° 0 dB, 0° \(Q\) (+20 log Q dB) Band-pass \(G_0\,(s/Q\omega_0)/D\) +20 dB/dec, +90° −20 dB/dec, −90° 0 dB, 0° (the lines meet at −20 log Q dB) Notch (notch) \(G_0\,(1 + s^2/\omega_0^2)/D\) 0 dB, 0° 0 dB, 0° zero: \(-\infty\) dB All-pass (all-pass) \(G_0\,(1 - s/Q\omega_0 + s^2/\omega_0^2)/D\) 0 dB, 0° 0 dB, −360° 0 dB, −180° Three rows deserve attention. In the low-pass and the high-pass, the two lines meet at \(f_0\) at 0 dB, and the real curve sits \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above: the error at the corner is the one from the previous note. In the band-pass, the lines meet at \(f_0\), but at \(-20\log_{10} Q\) dB, while the real curve is 0 dB there: the error is \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB, with the opposite sign. In the notch, the zero is at \(\pm j\omega_0\), undamped, so the notch is infinitely deep; its width is \(f_0/Q\). The all-pass has magnitude 1 at every frequency: the numerator is the conjugate of the denominator at \(s = j\omega\). Only the phase changes, from 0° to −360°, passing −180° at \(f_0\).

title: Second-order filters: the catalogue
heading: In the converters
summary: The five second-order filters with a pole pair, each as a factored form with f₀ and Q, and the asymptote that identifies it on the Bode plot.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: The buck's output filter is a low-pass: the switching voltage reaches the output attenuated above \(f_0\), at −40 dB per decade. With 22 µH, 47 µF and a 9 Ω load, \(f_0 = 4.96\) kHz and \(Q = 7.1\) (Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q). The function \(G_{vd}\) is not a pure low-pass: the ESR zero, at 677 kHz, gives back +20 dB per decade above it (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)). The other four filters do not appear in the lab's plant. The examples below are generic textbook cases, and serve only to recognise the shape on the Bode plot. Exercise A band-pass has \(f_0 = 1\) kHz and \(Q = 5\). Before drawing: at what level do the two asymptotes meet at \(f_0\), and what is the real magnitude there? title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
heading: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: The buck's LC filter stores energy in two elements, and the energy passes from one to the other: the response oscillates. A real first-order pole does not oscillate; for that you need a pair of complex poles.

title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
heading: The standard form
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad s_{1,2} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2Q} \pm j\,\omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4Q^2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2\zeta}\] Two numbers describe the pair: \(f_0\), the frequency of the pair, the distance of the poles from the origin (in hertz, on the \(s/2\pi\) plane); \(Q\), the quality factor, which says how lightly damped the pair is. The classical textbooks use the damping coefficient \(\zeta\), and, for the lossless pair, the bridge is \(\zeta = 1/(2Q)\), or \(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\). This course uses \(Q\), because it reads directly on the Bode plot.

title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
heading: Where the poles are
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: The value of \(Q\) decides the shape of the roots: \(Q < 0.5\): two distinct real poles, no oscillation; \(Q = 0.5\): a double real pole at \(-\omega_0\); \(Q > 0.5\): a complex conjugate pair. The higher the \(Q\), the closer to the \(j\omega\) axis; \(Q \to \infty\): the poles lie on the axis, at \(\pm j\omega_0\), and the response oscillates forever. For a complex pair, the imaginary part, \(\omega_0\sqrt{1 - 1/(4Q^2)}\), is the oscillation frequency, roughly \(f_0\) when \(Q\) is large. The real part, \(-\omega_0/(2Q)\), is the decay: the envelope falls with time constant \(2Q/\omega_0\).

title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
heading: On the Bode plot
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: The asymptotes of the pair are two lines: below \(f_0\), the magnitude stays at 0 dB (the DC gain) and the phase at 0°; above \(f_0\), the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade and the phase tends to −180°. At \(f_0\), the real phase is −90° for any \(Q\), because \(G(j\omega_0) = -jQ\). That is the point that organises the rest. Since the magnitude there is \(Q\), the real curve sits \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above the asymptote: that is the error at the corner. With \(Q = 1/\sqrt 2\) it is −3 dB, as for the first-order pole; with \(Q = 7\), +17 dB. The resonant peak exists only for \(Q > 0.707\), and its exact height is in the equation below. For a high \(Q\), it is almost \(Q\) in dB: \[\left|G(j\omega_{\mathrm{pico}})\right| = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{4Q^2}}}, \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{pico}} = \omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{2Q^2}}, \qquad Q > \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\] With \(Q = 5\), the exact peak is 14.02 dB, against 13.98 dB from the rule \(20\log_{10} Q\). With \(Q = 2\), the difference rises to 0.28 dB: the exact peak is 6.30 dB, and 6.02 dB is the rule \(20\log_{10} Q\). That is why the rule is a reading tool, valid for a high \(Q\). The phase has an error the rule does not show. With a high \(Q\), the phase turns almost entirely around \(f_0\): with \(Q = 7\), at \(0.9\,f_0\) the real phase is −34.1°, and a two-decade line, from 0° at \(f_0/10\) to −180° at \(10 f_0\), would give −86°.

title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
heading: In the step
summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: With a high \(Q\), the response overshoots the final value, comes back and oscillates around it. The overshoot follows from \(\zeta = 1/(2Q)\), through the classical formula \(e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\): \[M_p = e^{-\pi/\sqrt{4Q^2 - 1}}\] It is 44 % for \(Q = 2\), 16 % for \(Q = 1\), 4.3 % for \(Q = 0.707\), and zero for \(Q \le 0.5\). A pole pair with f₀ of 1 kHz: change Q with the control, or drag the pair, and watch the peak, the phase and the overshoot.

title: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q

summary: A pole pair is described by f₀ and Q. In the Bode plot, Q gives the height of the resonant peak; in the step, the balance between oscillation and decay, with the overshoot.
text: The buck's LC, 22 µH and 47 µF, has \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 4.95\) kHz without losses; with the model's losses, the exact pair sits at 4.96 kHz. The \(Q\) depends on the load, because the load in parallel with the capacitor damps the pair: \[\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R + R_s}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R + R_s)}}{L + C\left[R\,(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + R_s R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] Load Poles (\(s/2\pi\)) \(Q\) Peak Overshoot to a step in \(d\) \(2Q/\omega_0\) 4.5 Ω (2 A) \(-539 \pm j\,4939\) Hz 4.6 13.3 dB 71 % 0.30 ms 9 Ω (1 A) \(-351 \pm j\,4947\) Hz 7.1 17.0 dB 80 % 0.45 ms 90 Ω (0.1 A) \(-182 \pm j\,4947\) Hz 13.6 22.7 dB 89 % 0.88 ms The numbers come from the averaged model, without the loop: a step in the duty cycle would make the buck's output pass 80 % of the jump, oscillating with a 202 µs period. It first enters the 2 % band at 0.05 ms, but stays inside it only from 1.7 ms on. That is why the buck needs a loop that damps the pair (Feedback and margins). In the boost, the resonance, seen through \(D'\), drops to 690 Hz, with \(Q = 4.4\) at 1 A and 3.6 at 2 A, with 25 mΩ of resistance in series with the inductor and an ESR of 10 mΩ (without the ESR, 4.5 and 3.7; Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost). title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: Transfer function and factored form
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: This note opens the unit Read the plant. It teaches one skill: write a converter's plant in factored form, and recognise in each factor a frequency of the Bode plot. The starting equation is the buck's plant (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)): \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] It has three parts: a gain, a zero and a pair of poles. This note teaches you to name them.

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: A ratio of polynomials
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: In a linear, time-invariant system at rest at time zero, the ratio between the transform of the output and that of the input is a fixed function of the system: \[G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = \frac{N(s)}{D(s)}\] In the buck, the input is the small variation of the duty cycle, \(\hat d\), and the output is the small variation of the output voltage, \(\hat v_o\), around the operating point (The averaged switch model). The polynomials have real coefficients, and their roots have names: zeros are the roots of \(N(s)\): there, \(G(s) = 0\); poles are the roots of \(D(s)\): there, \(G(s)\) goes to infinity; the order is the degree of \(D(s)\). The buck is second order, because it stores energy in two elements, the inductor and the capacitor. In a circuit, the order does not exceed the number of these elements. Since the degree of \(N(s)\) does not exceed that of \(D(s)\), the function is proper: the gain does not grow without limit at high frequency. Circuits built from resistors, inductors and capacitors always give proper functions.

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: The factored form
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: Each real root becomes a factor \(1 + s/\omega\), which equals 1 at \(s = 0\). A pair of complex roots becomes \(1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2\), the second-order form. Putting it together, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\): \[G(s) = G_0\,\frac{\prod_i \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{z,i}}\right)\prod_k \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{Q_k\,\omega_k} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_k^2}\right)}{\prod_j \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{p,j}}\right)\prod_m \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{Q_m\,\omega_m} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_m^2}\right)}, \qquad G_0 = G(0)\] This is the form the course uses, and it has two advantages: the DC gain, \(G_0 = G(0)\), stands alone in front, because every factor equals 1 at \(s = 0\); each \(\omega\) is the frequency at which that factor starts to act: that is where it shows up on the Bode plot. With the form \(K/(s + a)\), the DC gain, \(K/a\), is hidden in the denominator. That is why the course writes everything factored, like \(G_{vd}\) above, where \(G_0 = V_{in}R/(R+R_s)\) is in plain sight. A root in the right half-plane enters with its sign changed. A zero in the right half-plane has the same magnitude as a zero in the left half-plane: only the phase differs (Right-half-plane zero). Pole or zero frequency The root at \(s = -\omega\) corresponds to the frequency \(\omega\), in rad/s, or \(f = \omega/2\pi\), in Hz: the pole or zero frequency. The figures in this course mark the s-plane axes in hertz, \(s/2\pi\).

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: The s-plane
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: Each root is a point in the complex plane. The real part says how the response decays: the further left of the \(j\omega\) axis, the faster. The imaginary part says whether the response oscillates, and at what frequency. A pole in the right half-plane would make the response grow without limit. In open loop, therefore, stability depends only on the poles. A zero in the right half-plane does not make the plant unstable, but it has an effect on the loop, which the note on the right-half-plane zero explains. Poles and zero of the buck's plant, from the averaged model: the complex pair near 5 kHz and the ESR zero far to the left, out of view. Change the load and the ESR and watch the roots move.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: The averaged switch model
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: To design the control we need a transfer function, but the switch turns on and off every \(T_s\) and has none. The way out is to look at the average of each quantity over one period, which varies slowly. This note does the derivation for the buck; the result is the plant of the next note.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 1: the switched circuit
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Let \(q(t) \in \{0, 1\}\) be the state of the high-side switch. The switching-node voltage is \(v_{sw} = q\,v_{in}\), and the current drawn from the input is \(i_{in} = q\,i_L\). On the inductor, with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) (in CCM there is always one switch in series with it): \[L\,\frac{di_L}{dt} = q\,v_{in} - v_o - R_s\,i_L\]

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 2: the average over one period
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Define the moving average \(\langle x \rangle_{T_s}(t) = \frac{1}{T_s}\int_{t - T_s}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\). The average of \(q\) is the duty ratio \(d\). If \(v_{in}\) and \(i_L\) barely change within one period (small ripple), the average of the product is the product of the averages, and the switch pair becomes the averaged switching cell: \[\langle v_{sw} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle v_{in} \rangle_{T_s}, \qquad \langle i_{in} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle i_L \rangle_{T_s}\] Averaged switch model The averaged cell is an ideal transformer of ratio \(1 : d\), with a variable \(d\): the voltage comes out multiplied by \(d\), and the input current is the inductor's multiplied by \(d\). Power is conserved: \(\langle v_{in}\rangle\langle i_{in}\rangle = \langle v_{sw}\rangle\langle i_L\rangle\). Replacing the cell in the circuit, the inductor equation becomes \[L\,\frac{d\langle i_L\rangle}{dt} = d\,\langle v_{in}\rangle - \langle v_o\rangle - R_s\,\langle i_L\rangle\] and the capacitor, the ESR and the load stay as before, with the averaged quantities. The ripple vanishes by construction.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 3: the operating point
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In steady state, the derivatives vanish: \(\langle i_L\rangle = I_L = V_o/R\) and \(D\,V_{in} = V_o + R_s I_L\), that is, \(D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\cdot\frac{R + R_s}{R}\), the duty ratio with losses.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 4: perturbation
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Write each quantity as its operating point plus a small perturbation: \(d = D + \hat d\), \(v_{in} = V_{in} + \hat v_{in}\), \(i_L = I_L + \hat i_L\), \(v_o = V_o + \hat v_o\). The only nonlinear term is the product \(d\,v_{in}\): \[d\,v_{in} = D V_{in} + V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} + \hat d\,\hat v_{in}\]

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 5: linearization
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The term \(\hat d\,\hat v_{in}\) is the product of two small perturbations and is neglected. Subtracting the operating point leaves a linear equation: \[L\,\frac{d\hat i_L}{dt} = V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} - \hat v_o - R_s\,\hat i_L\] The switching node becomes a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\hat d + D\hat v_{in}\) that drives the LC filter. With a constant \(V_{in}\) (\(\hat v_{in} = 0\)), the buck is linear in \(d\) and the linearization is exact: the plant \(\hat v_o/\hat d\) is \(V_{in}\) times the filter's transfer function, which leads to (2) in The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] Why the boost is different In the boost, the cell multiplies the state variables: \(\langle v_{sw}\rangle = d'\,\langle v_o\rangle\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,\langle i_L\rangle\). Linearization leaves terms \(V_o\hat d\) and \(I_L\hat d\), and the second one creates the right-half-plane zero. The resulting plant is in Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Where averaging stops being valid
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The averaged model assumes two things, and each has a limit. Small ripple. The average of a product is only the product of the averages if \(\Delta i_L\) and \(\Delta v_o\) are small next to the averages. The model does not see the ripple, but the ADC does: it samples at a fixed point of the waveform and reads a constant offset (see Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM). Slow variations. The average only describes perturbations much slower than the switching. A perturbation near \(f_s/2\) creates, at the switching node, a component at \(f_s - f\) of almost the same frequency, which the filter lets through and which is confused with it by sampling. In practice, the model holds up to a fraction of \(f_s/2\), and the loop's crossover stays well below that. The model also does not know the control is digital: the sample, the computation and the PWM delay the response by \((1 + D)T_s\), the computation delay, which enters as a factor \(e^{-s(1+D)T_s}\) multiplying the plant. DCM and diode emulation In DCM, the current rests at zero for part of the period and the averaged cell changes: the plant loses one of the LC poles. The synchronous buck stays in forced CCM and does not have this problem, unless the firmware turns the low-side switch off on negative current.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: In the converters
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the lab's buck (24 V → 9 V, 200 kHz), \(R_s\) = 30 mΩ + 10 mΩ = 40 mΩ, and at 1 A the duty ratio with losses is \((9 + 0.04)/24 = 0.377\), against 0.375 ideal. The averaged model with the \((1+D)T_s\) delay was checked in QSPICE by adding a small sine to the duty inside the firmware: it stayed within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of the switched circuit from 500 Hz to 15 kHz, across the resonance. At 30 kHz, already almost a third of \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz, the magnitude still matches, but the phase is 3.9° off and the point fails the linearity check (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). The 2p2z's crossover, at 8 kHz, lies in the region where the model is reliable. In the boost and the buck-boost, with the right-half-plane zero, the same method gave 0.2 dB and 1.4° and 0.4 dB and 1.9°, from 300 Hz to 7 kHz. title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example
heading: Specifications
summary: The lab's boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step, the right-half-plane zero that holds the crossover at 1.5 kHz and the fifteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: Quantity Value Input / output 12 V → 48 V Switching 100 kHz, dead time of 100 ns Inductor 33 µH, resistance of 15 mΩ Capacitor 100 µF, ESR of 10 mΩ Switches \(R_{on}\) = 10 mΩ Load 48 Ω (1 A) and 24 Ω (2 A) ADC 12 bits, full scale of 60 V Duty ratio from 0 to 0.85 Design summary. title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example
heading: The example, step by step
summary: The lab's boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step, the right-half-plane zero that holds the crossover at 1.5 kHz and the fifteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: Steady state. The volt-second balance of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM, applied to the boost, gives \(D = 1 - 12/48 = 0.75\); with the losses, 0.752 at 1 A and 0.754 at 2 A. The inductor current is \(I_o/D'\): 4.03 A and 8.14 A. The ripple is \(\Delta i_L = V_{in} D T_s/L = 2.73\) A (2.71 A in QSPICE), and the capacitor's, \(I_o D T_s/C = 75\) mV at 1 A; with the ESR steps, the simulated output has 102 mV peak to peak. Sizing L and C. The capacitor is set by the load step: \(1\,\text{A}/(2\pi\cdot 1.5\,\text{kHz}\cdot 100\,\text{µF}) = 1.06\) V. In the simulation with the 2p2z, the output falls from 47.95 to 46.89 V: 1.06 V. With the boost's low crossover, the capacitor has to be large. The averaged switch model. The boost's averaged cell multiplies the state variables: \(d'\,v\) and \(d'\,i_L\). \(R_l\) = 15 mΩ + 10 mΩ = 25 mΩ. The model stayed within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, at 48 and 24 Ω (1 and 2 A), measured as in Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty. Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost. DC gain of 190 (45.6 dB), about \(V/D'\); resonance at 690 Hz, with \(Q\) = 4.4 at 1 A and 3.6 at 2 A; at 1.5 kHz, the plant is 34.1 dB. The right-half-plane zero. The right-half-plane zero lies at 14.1 kHz at 1 A and 6.9 kHz at 2 A. At 1.5 kHz, it takes 6.1° and 12.3° of phase. The ESR zero (The ESR zero) lies at 159 kHz and gives only 0.5°. Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost. The sample, just before G1 turns on, sits about 50 mV above the average: with the samples at 48 V, the average is 47.95 V. In the plant the ADC sees, the right-half-plane zero rises to 22.1 kHz at 1 A and 8.4 kHz at 2 A, and the margin gains 1.6°. Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins. With the 2p2z, the crossover is at 1.5 kHz, with a phase margin of 45.3° and a gain margin of 17.5 dB at 1 A (the phase crosses −180° at 8.4 kHz); at 2 A, 40.6° and 13.4 dB (6.1 kHz). Computation and PWM delay. The delay is \((1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s = 14.5\) µs and costs \(360^\circ\cdot 1.5\,\text{kHz}\cdot 14.5\,\text{µs} = 7.8^\circ\). With \(f_s\) = 100 kHz (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)), the crossover sits at \(f_s/67\): here the limit is the zero, not the delay. Robust design across the operating range. The 1.5 kHz crossover sits at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\) at 2 A. With the input at 10 V and 2 A, the zero comes down to 4.7 kHz, the crossover to 1.27 kHz, and the margin to 34.7°. The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping. Without prewarping, Tustin would take 1.5 kHz to 1.499 kHz, but the 30 kHz pole to 24.1 kHz (−20 %). The 2p2z was discretized by matched poles and zeros. The 2p2z compensator. The zeros go to \(e^{-2\pi\cdot 500\cdot 10\,\text{µs}} = 0.9691\) and the pole to \(p = 0.1518\): \(b_0 = 0.1648\), \(b_1 = -0.3194\), \(b_2 = 0.1548\), \(a_1 = -1.1518\) and \(a_2 = 0.1518\). title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The buck connects the switching node to the input, then to ground, and the LC filter delivers the average of that square wave to the load. This note computes the duty ratio and the ripple in steady state. It is the first step of the digital buck trail. Synchronous buck: the high-side switch conducts for D·Tₛ and the low-side switch for the rest of the period.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Volt-second balance
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In steady state, the inductor current ends each period at the value it started with. Since \(v_L = L\,di_L/dt\), the area of the inductor voltage over one period is zero: \[(V_{in} - V_o)\,D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D)\,T_s = 0\] With the high-side switch closed, the inductor sees \(V_{in} - V_o\); with it open (and the low-side switch closed), it sees \(-V_o\). Solving: \[D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\] Duty ratio The duty ratio \(D\) is the fraction of the switching period \(T_s = 1/f_s\) during which the high-side switch conducts. We write \(D' = 1 - D\) for the rest of the period. The resistive losses (\(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\), in series with the inductor) call for slightly more \(D\), because part of the voltage drops across them. In closed loop this does not matter: the controller finds the \(D\) that gives \(V_o\) on its own.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Inductor current ripple
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: During \(DT_s\), the current rises with slope \((V_{in} - V_o)/L\); during \(D'T_s\), it falls with slope \(V_o/L\). The peak-to-peak ripple is \[\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{L\,f_s}\] The average of \(i_L\) is the load current \(I_o = V_o/R\), because in steady state the capacitor accumulates no charge. The peak, \(I_o + \Delta i_L/2\), is what saturates the core and what the switches must withstand.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: The boundary of continuous conduction
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Continuous conduction mode (CCM) In CCM, the inductor current never rests at zero during the period. The boundary is \(I_o = \Delta i_L/2\): below it, the valley of the triangular wave would reach zero. In a buck with a diode, below the boundary the diode blocks and the converter enters discontinuous conduction (DCM), with another duty ratio and other dynamics. The synchronous buck is different: the low-side switch conducts in both directions, the current goes negative in the valley and the converter stays in CCM, called forced CCM. The equations of this note hold at any load. Negative current in the synchronous buck At light load, or in a downward reference step, the negative current returns energy to the input. A bench supply that cannot sink current may see its voltage rise. Controllers with "diode emulation" turn the low-side switch off when the current reaches zero, and the converter then enters DCM again.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Output voltage ripple
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The capacitor absorbs the AC part of \(i_L\), a triangle of \(\pm\Delta i_L/2\). The charge it receives in the positive half is the area of a triangle, \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{T_s}{2}\cdot\frac{\Delta i_L}{2}\), and the capacitive part follows from it. The capacitor's series resistance adds a part proportional to the current itself: \[\Delta v_C = \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,C\,f_s}, \qquad \Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}} = R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,\Delta i_L\] The two parts are out of phase: the ESR's follows the current, and the capacitive one is its integral, with peaks a quarter period apart. The total ripple lies between the larger one and their sum. The next step, Sizing L and C, uses these equations backwards: from the ripple specifications to L and C.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: In the converters
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The lab's buck goes from 24 V to 9 V at 200 kHz, with L = 22 µH and C = 47 µF (ESR 5 mΩ). \(D = 9/24 = 0.375\). \(\Delta i_L = (24 - 9)\cdot 0.375 / (22\,\text{µH}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz}) = 1.28\) A. With the 9 Ω load (1 A), the current goes from 0.36 A to 1.64 A; with 4.5 Ω (2 A), the peak reaches 2.64 A. The CCM boundary is at \(I_o = 0.64\) A, that is, a load above 14.1 Ω. \(\Delta v_C = 1.28/(8\cdot 47\,\text{µF}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz}) = 17.0\) mV and \(\Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}} = 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 1.28\,\text{A} = 6.4\) mV. Adding the waveforms with the right phase, the total is 17.6 mV peak to peak, not 23.4 mV. In the QSPICE simulation, before the load step, each period shows \(\Delta i_L \approx 1.28\) A and about 18 mV of output ripple. The ADC samples at the start of the period, in the current's valley. With ideal waveforms, that point sits about 6 mV below the average; in the simulation it is about 5 mV, one ADC step (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) and ADC quantization). title: The ESR zero
heading: The ESR zero
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: A real capacitor has an equivalent series resistance (ESR). In the buck's plant, it appears as the factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator of (1): a real zero in the left half-plane. \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\]

title: The ESR zero
heading: Where the zero comes from
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The impedance of the capacitor with its ESR is \[Z_C(s) = R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + \frac{1}{sC} = \frac{1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C}{sC}\] Below \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\), \(1/sC\) dominates, and the capacitor filters. Above it, \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) dominates, and the capacitor becomes a resistor: the current ripple now produces a proportional voltage ripple, the \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\Delta i_L\) part of equation Output voltage ripple of the buck. ESR zero The ESR zero is the frequency at which the two parts of the capacitor's impedance have equal magnitude. Above it, the buck's plant falls 20 dB per decade instead of 40, and the phase rises by up to 90° relative to the pole pair alone.

title: The ESR zero
heading: What the zero does on the Bode plot
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: A left-half-plane zero lifts the phase: \(\arctan(f/f_{\mathrm{ESR}})\), which is 45° at \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) and almost nothing a decade below. If the zero is near the crossover \(f_c\), it supplies for free part of the phase boost the compensator would have to give. That was the case in older bucks with electrolytic capacitors, whose ESR is tens of milliohms: with them, a type II compensator was enough. With ceramic capacitors, the ESR drops to a few milliohms, and the zero moves up to hundreds of kHz, above \(f_s/2\). There it does not help: the digital loop does not even see frequencies above \(f_s/2\) (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)), and the compensator must give all the phase boost, with two zeros, like the The 2p2z compensator. Do not count on the ESR An electrolytic's ESR varies with temperature (it may double in the cold) and grows with aging. A design that relies on the ESR zero for its phase margin may lose it in winter or after a few years. And putting a ceramic in parallel, to lower the ripple, moves the zero and changes the whole plant. ESR on purpose A resistor is sometimes added in series with the capacitor just to create the zero. It works, but the cost shows in the output ripple and in the load-step response, which gains an instantaneous jump of \(\Delta I\cdot R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\).

title: The ESR zero
heading: In the converters
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the lab's buck, C = 47 µF with an ESR of 5 mΩ: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 47\,\text{µF}} = 677\ \text{kHz}\] That is 3.4 times the 200 kHz switching frequency. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the zero gives 0.7° of phase; even at \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz it gives only 8.4°. For the loop, the capacitor is ideal, and the compensator does all the work. In the boost and the buck-boost, C = 100 µF with an ESR of 10 mΩ, and the zero lies at 159 kHz, also above the 100 kHz switching frequency. There the ESR shows up another way: the ADC samples just before switch G1 turns on, when the capacitor carries the whole inductor current, and reads \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) times that current above the average. The model validated in QSPICE includes this term (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). Exercise What ESR would put the buck's zero at 8 kHz, on the crossover? How large would the ESR part of the output ripple be? Exercise A 220 µF electrolytic has an ESR of 80 mΩ at 25 °C. Where is the zero? And if the ESR doubles in the cold? title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: Four-switch buck-boost
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: An 8 to 16 V battery feeding a 12 V bus must step the voltage down and up. The four-switch buck-boost does both with a single inductor, without inverting the output: a buck leg at the input (Q1 on top, Q2 below, node A) and a boost leg at the output (Q3 on top, Q4 below, node B), with the inductor between the two nodes. The lab's four-switch buck-boost: the input leg (Q1, Q2) and the output leg (Q3, Q4), with the inductor between nodes A and B.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: Three modes
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Buck. Q3 stays on and Q4 off; only the input leg switches. It is a buck: \(V = D\,V_{in}\), the inductor current is the load's, and the plant has no right-half-plane zero. Boost. Q1 stays on and Q2 off; only the output leg switches. It is a boost: \(V = V_{in}/(1 - D)\), with the right-half-plane zero. Buck-boost. Both legs switch together: G1 turns on Q1 and Q4, and the inductor receives the input; G2 turns on Q2 and Q3, and the inductor discharges into the output. From the volt-second balance, \(D\,V_{in} = D'\,V\), that is, \(V/V_{in} = D/D'\). The first two modes have lower losses, but the firmware must decide which mode it is in and switch modes when \(V_{in}\) crosses \(V\), where each one's duty reaches its limit. The third covers the whole range with a single duty, without transitions. The price is that all four switches commutate every period and the inductor carries the input and output currents added together, \(I = I_o/D'\). The lab's mode The lab's converter always runs in buck-boost mode: G1 drives Q1 and Q4, G2 drives Q2 and Q3. The firmware is the same as the buck's and the boost's, with one duty and one voltage loop. The small-signal model and every number on this site are for that mode.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: The plant in buck-boost mode
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With G1, the inductor sees \(+v_{in}\); with G2, \(-v\). The averaged cell becomes \(L\,di_L/dt = d\,v_{in} - d'\,v - R_l\,i_L\), and the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L\), as in the boost. Linearizing with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\), \(\hat d\) switches the voltage \(V_{in} + V\) across the inductor, instead of the boost's \(V\): \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\] Here \(R_l\) adds the inductor and the two switches always in series with it. The right-half-plane zero has the same origin as in the boost, the \(I(sL + R_l)\) term: \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I R_l}{2\pi I L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\cdot\frac{V_{in} + V}{V}\] As in the boost, the resonance is that of the inductor seen through \(D'\), \(f_0 \approx D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). The ADC sample also reads the ESR term of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, and the delay that best fits QSPICE is the same, \((1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s\).

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: The plant changes with the input
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With the output fixed, the input sets \(D\): from \(V/(V_{in} + V)\), 0.57 at 9 V to 0.44 at 15 V, without losses. Hence: The resonance rises with \(D'\), about 30 % from 9 to 15 V. The DC gain hardly changes: without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = (V_{in} + V)/D'\), and both quantities grow together. The right-half-plane zero comes down when the input falls and when the load rises. The worst case is the minimum input with the maximum load. A fixed compensator must work at all these points; how to choose it is in Robust design across the operating range.
