title: Sizing L and C
heading: Sizing L and C
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: This procedure uses the equations of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM backwards: it starts from the specifications and arrives at L and C. At the end, we check the lab's buck.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 1. Choose the current ripple and compute L
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Define the relative ripple \(r = \Delta i_L / I_{o,\max}\). Values from 20 % to 40 % are the usual starting point: less calls for a large, slow inductor; more raises the peak, the core losses and the capacitor's RMS current. From the ripple equation, \[L = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{r\,I_{o,\max}\,f_s}\] Use the highest input voltage: \(1 - D\) grows with \(V_{in}\), and so does the ripple. Saturation Check the peak \(I_{o,\max} + \Delta i_L/2\) against the inductor's saturation current, not only against its rated current. The inductance of many powdered-iron inductors drops 20 % to 30 % with current, and the ripple rises in the same proportion.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 2. Compute C and the maximum ESR from the voltage ripple
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: With the specified output ripple \(\Delta v_o\), split the budget between the two parts: \[C \ge \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,f_s\,\Delta v_o}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{ESR}} \le \frac{\Delta v_o}{\Delta i_L}\] With ceramic capacitors, the ESR is a few milliohms and the capacitive part dominates. With electrolytics, the ESR usually dominates, and the capacitance ends up well above the minimum. Remember that the parts are out of phase: requiring each one below \(\Delta v_o\) already leaves some margin. Ceramic capacitance under bias An X5R or X7R ceramic loses a good part of its capacitance with the applied DC voltage. Use the manufacturer's curve at the output voltage, not the rated value.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 3. Check the capacitor's RMS current
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The buck's output capacitor carries the triangular part of \(i_L\): \[I_{C,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{\Delta i_L}{\sqrt{12}}\] Compare it with the capacitor's rated RMS current (or that of the bank), at the working temperature.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 4. Check the load step and the resonance
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Ripple rarely sets C. In a load step \(\Delta I\), the capacitor supplies the difference until the loop reacts, and the loop reacts in about \(1/(2\pi f_c)\). A first-order estimate of the dip is \[\Delta V \approx \frac{\Delta I}{2\pi\,f_c\,C}\] where \(f_c\) is the crossover frequency of the loop gain. Finally, compute the resonance \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) of the plant: it must lie well below \(f_s/2\) and preferably below \(f_c\), because the compensator will have to cancel its pole pair.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: The right-half-plane zero
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the buck, raising the duty raises the voltage applied to the LC filter, and the output rises. In the boost, the same action has two opposite effects. The main switch stays on longer, the inductor builds up more current, and the output will rise; but while the switch is on, the inductor is cut off from the output. At first, the inductor current is still the same, but it reaches the output during a smaller fraction of the period, \(D' - \hat d\): the output receives \(I\hat d\) less and falls. Only later, when the inductor current grows, does it rise. A response that starts in the opposite direction to where it ends is the signature of a right-half-plane zero.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: The boost's plant
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: From the averaged model in continuous conduction, with the losses \(R_l\) of the inductor and one switch, the capacitor with its ESR and the load \(R\), the transfer function from the duty to the output is \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\] The numerator vanishes when \(D'V = I(sL + R_l)\). With \(I = V/(RD')\), the inductor current, the zero sits at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\): \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{2\pi L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\] Right-half-plane zero A zero at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), with \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}} > 0\). Like an ordinary zero, it makes the magnitude rise by 20 dB per decade above \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\); but, like a pole, it lags the phase by up to \(90^\circ\). In a step, it makes the response start in the wrong direction.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: Why it limits the crossover
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: An ordinary zero in the left half-plane helps the compensator: it gives gain and phase lead. The right-half-plane zero gives the gain and takes the phase, like a delay. The compensator cannot cancel it, because that would take a pole in the right half-plane, an unstable controller. What is left is to cross well below it: at \(f_c\), it already takes \(\arctan(f_c/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\), and this lag adds to the firmware's (Computation and PWM delay). Rules of thumb say to cross between a third and a fifth of the zero in the worst case: at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\), it takes 18.4° of phase; at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\), 11.3°. Neither is a limit: what decides is the margin at the worst corner, adding up the zero, the delay and the lead the compensator still gives there (Robust design across the operating range). And the worst case is the maximum load with the minimum input: smaller \(R\) and \(D'\), lower zero. Unlike the buck's, the boost's plant changes a lot with the operating point, and the margins must be checked at all of them (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). Loop gain of the boost with the 2p2z: the crossover stays at 1.5 kHz, well below the right-half-plane zero More gain does not make the boost faster With a slow boost, the temptation is to raise the gain. Near the zero, the phase falls fast (26.6° at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/2\), 45° at it), the margin disappears, and the loop starts ringing on the load step, precisely where the current is highest and the zero lowest.

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the buck, the duty only multiplies the input, and the plant is \(V_{in}\) times the LC filter (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)). In the boost, the averaged cell multiplies the state variables: the switch node is \(d'\,v\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,i_L\), with \(d' = 1 - d\) (The averaged switch model). The plant inherits three differences from this: the gain depends on \(D'\), so does the resonance, and a right-half-plane zero appears.

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: From the averaged model to the plant
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus one switch's, the averaged equations of the inductor and the capacitor, perturbed and linearized with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\), become \[(sL + R_l)\,\hat i_L = V\hat d - D'\hat v, \qquad \hat v = Z_o\,(D'\,\hat i_L - I\,\hat d)\] with \(Z_o = R \parallel (R_{ESR} + 1/sC)\) and \(I\) the average inductor current. The first term of each equation comes from \(d\) multiplying \(v\) and \(i_L\): these are the \(V\hat d\) and \(I\hat d\) terms the buck does not have. Eliminating \(\hat i_L\): \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\]

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: DC gain, resonance and Q
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: At \(s = 0\), \(Z_o = R\) and, without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = V/D'\). At 48 V with \(D' \approx 0.25\), that gives about 190 V per unit of duty: eight times the gain of the lab's buck. The denominator is the LC filter with the inductor seen through \(D'^2\), as an inductance \(L/D'^2\). The pair of poles lies at \[\omega_0 \approx \frac{D'}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{\omega_0}{1/(RC) + R_l/L},\] and comes down when the input falls and \(D'\) shrinks. The damping comes from the load, \(1/(RC)\), and from the losses, \(R_l/L\). Effective inductance In the boost's averaged model, the inductor \(L\) seen from the output is \(L/D'^2\). With \(D' = 0.25\), the lab's 33 µH behave as 530 µH in the output filter: the resonance is four times lower than \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\).

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: The right-half-plane zero
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.

text: The numerator vanishes at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\): \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{2\pi L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\] Above \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), the magnitude stops falling at 40 dB per decade and the phase keeps falling: the zero adds up to \(-90^\circ\) to the \(-180^\circ\) of the pair of poles. The physics and the limit it puts on the crossover are in The right-half-plane zero. The ESR zero, in the left half-plane, lies at \(1/(2\pi R_{ESR} C)\) = 159 kHz, above the switching frequency, as in the buck (The ESR zero).

trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: From the circuit to the transfer function
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The inductor and the series resistance form \(Z_L = sL + R_s\), with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\). The capacitor with its ESR, in parallel with the load, forms \(Z_o = (R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + 1/sC)\parallel R\). The plant is a voltage divider: \[G_{vd}(s) = V_{in}\,\frac{Z_o}{Z_L + Z_o} = V_{in}\,\frac{R\,(1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C)}{\alpha_2 s^2 + \alpha_1 s + \alpha_0}\] with \[\alpha_2 = LC\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}), \qquad \alpha_0 = R + R_s\] \[\alpha_1 = L + C\left[R R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + R_s(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\right]\] Arranged in the canonical second-order form: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] It has three ingredients: the DC gain \(V_{in}R/(R + R_s) \approx V_{in}\), the LC's complex pole pair and the ESR zero.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: The resonance and the Q
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The pole pair sits at the filter's resonance, with a quality factor set by the damping: \[\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R + R_s}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R + R_s)}}{L + C\left[R\,(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + R_s R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] Quality factor \(Q\) measures how lightly damped the pole pair is. On the Bode plot, the magnitude rises about \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above the DC gain at \(f_0\), and the phase drops 180° over a band about \(f_0/Q\) wide. In time, the response rings at \(f_0\) and decays with a time constant \(2Q/\omega_0\). Two sources of damping add like conductances: the load in parallel with the capacitor, with \(Q_R = R/Z_0\), and the series resistances, with \(Q_s = Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\). Hence the dependence on the load: heavy load (small R) damps more, and \(Q\) falls; light load (large R) damps less, and \(Q\) rises up to the limit \(Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\), set by the losses alone; the DC gain and \(f_0\) barely change with the load. Above \(f_0\), the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade and the phase stays near −180°. This is the phase the compensator must lift, with zeros near the resonance, for there to be phase margin at crossover (see Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins and The 2p2z compensator). The buck's plant: resonant peak near 5 kHz and a 40 dB per decade roll-off; the phase includes the digital loop's (1+D)Tₛ delay. The peak depends on the load Design the compensator at the lightest load the converter will see. That is where the resonant peak is highest, and where the loop gain may cross 0 dB again with little phase.

heading: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.

text: This note puts together everything the trail has built. The 2p2z compensator becomes the difference equation below, the saturation of Anti-windup and duty saturation sits at the output, and the arithmetic is that of Q15 fixed point: \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\]

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: The sequence in each period
summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The timer reaches the end of the period and generates the update event. That event triggers the ADC. The ADC finishes the conversion and calls the interrupt. The interrupt computes the error and the new duty, and saturates it. It writes the CCR. With preload on, the new value only takes effect in the next period. Step 4 is what scenario.cpp imitates with s->duty = s->pending: the duty computed from period \(k\)'s sample governs period \(k+1\). With trailing-edge PWM, the edge that matters comes \(D\,T_s\) into that period, and the total delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s\), the subject of Computation and PWM delay.

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: Float variant (Cortex-M4F, M33)
summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: This is scenario.cpp's logic, with the error in volts and the coefficients of the buck's default design. That firmware stores the pole \(p = a_2\) as the controller's fourth value and computes with it, and this variant also stores only \(a_2\): #include "stm32g4xx.h" /* or your MCU's CMSIS header */ #define PWM_N 850u /* 170 MHz / 200 kHz; ARR = 849 */ #define LSB (20.0f / 4095.0f) #define DMIN 0.0f #define DMAX 0.9f static const float b0 = 0.23114164f, b1 = -0.43413087f, b2 = 0.20384645f; static const float a2 = 0.15183580f; /* = p; a1 = -(1 + a2) = -1.15183580 */ static float u1 = 0.375f, u2 = 0.375f, e1, e2; /* start at the steady-state duty */ static volatile float vref = 9.0f; void ADC1_2_IRQHandler(void) { GPIOB->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BS0; /* measurement pin: high */ float e = vref - (float)ADC1->DR * LSB; /* reading DR clears the end-of-conversion flag */ float u = u1 + a2 * (u1 - u2) + b0 * e + b1 * e1 + b2 * e2; if (u < DMIN) u = DMIN; /* store the saturated value: anti-windup */ if (u > DMAX) u = DMAX; u2 = u1; u1 = u; e2 = e1; e1 = e; TIM1->CCR1 = (uint32_t)(u * PWM_N + 0.5f); /* preload: takes effect next period */ GPIOB->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BR0; /* measurement pin: low */ } u1 + a2*(u1 - u2) is the same as -a1*u1 - a2*u2, because \(a_1 = -(1 + a_2)\): it is the velocity form, which computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to u1. Written this way, it does without \(a_1 = -1.15\), which does not fit in Q15 in the fixed-point variant, and the integrator stays exactly at \(z = 1\). The reference can also get the slew of Anti-windup and duty saturation, by adding a limited step to vref in each interrupt.

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: Fixed-point variant (Cortex-M0+)
summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The error stays in ADC codes, the duty in timer counts with 13 fraction bits, and the coefficients in Q2.13, in counts per code, as in the table of Q15 fixed point: #define FRAC 13 #define REF_CODE 1843 /* 9 V * 4095 / 20 V = 1842.75 */ static const int32_t b0q = 7861, b1q = -14764, b2q = 6932; /* Q2.13 */ static const int32_t a2q = 4975; /* a2 = p in Q15; a1 = -(1 + a2) */ static const int32_t UMAX = 765 << FRAC; /* 0.9 * 850 counts */ static int32_t uq1 = 319 << FRAC, uq2 = 319 << FRAC; /* 0.375 * 850 */ static int32_t eq1, eq2; void ADC1_IRQHandler(void) { int32_t e = REF_CODE - (int32_t)ADC1->DR; /* error in codes: can be 0 */ int64_t acc = (int64_t)uq1 + (((int64_t)a2q * (uq1 - uq2) + (1 << 14)) >> 15) + (int64_t)b0q * e + (int64_t)b1q * eq1 + (int64_t)b2q * eq2; if (acc < 0) acc = 0; /* saturate in Q13 counts */ if (acc > UMAX) acc = UMAX; uq2 = uq1; uq1 = (int32_t)acc; eq2 = eq1; eq1 = e; TIM1->CCR1 = (uint32_t)((acc + (1 << (FRAC - 1))) >> FRAC); } The states keep the 13 fraction bits. Without them, the integrator's steps, thousandths of a count, would round to zero, as DPWM resolution and limit cycles warns.

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: The timing budget
summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: At 170 MHz, a 5 µs period has 850 cycles. Out of that time come the ADC conversion, which starts at the beginning of the period, the interrupt entry (12 cycles on the Cortex-M4 with no wait states, according to the manual) and the computation itself. The CCR must be written before the end of the period. The 2p2z equation, as written above, has four multiplications and five additions or subtractions; with the ADC and CCR scaling, about ten operations, typically a few tens of cycles with the FPU. Even with the peripheral accesses, the interrupt uses a small fraction of the period. But don't trust estimates: measure. GPIO pin: the pair of BSRR writes above makes a pulse whose width is the interrupt's duration. On the scope, next to the PWM, you also see the latency from the start of the period and the variation from one period to the next. Cycle counter: on the Cortex-M3, M4 and M7, the DWT counts clock cycles. The M0 and M0+ lack that counter; use the pin there. CoreDebug->DEMCR |= CoreDebug_DEMCR_TRCENA_Msk; /* once, at initialization */ DWT->CYCCNT = 0; DWT->CTRL |= DWT_CTRL_CYCCNTENA_Msk; uint32_t t0 = DWT->CYCCNT; /* at the start of the interrupt */ /* ... */ uint32_t dt = DWT->CYCCNT - t0; /* at the end; unsigned subtraction survives wraparound */ if (dt > worst) worst = dt; /* keep the worst case, not the average */ Preload off Without preload (the OC1PE bit on the STM32), the new CCR takes effect at once. If it is written below the counter's current value, that period's compare has already passed, and the pulse may come out doubled or not at all. Turn preload on and accept the period of delay, which the design of Computation and PWM delay already includes. Fast code On the STM32G4, run the interrupt from CCM SRAM, without flash wait states. Declare the routine's state static, and don't call library functions inside it.

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: The 2p2z compensator
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The buck's plant, above the LC resonance, has a phase near \(-180^\circ\) (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)), and the digital delay takes even more (Computation and PWM delay). An integrator alone would add \(-90^\circ\), and the loop would have no margin. The compensator needs an integrator, to drive the steady-state error to zero, and two zeros, to give phase back at the crossover. That is the 2p2z: two poles, two zeros. \[C(z) = K\,\frac{(1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_2 z^{-1})}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})}, \qquad z_i = e^{-2\pi f_{zi} T_s}, \quad p = e^{-2\pi f_p T_s}\] The two poles are the integrator, at \(z = 1\), and a real high-frequency pole \(p\). It is the digital version of the analog type III compensator, which has two high-frequency poles instead of one.

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: Design by poles and zeros
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Each root has a job, and the design is done on the Bode plot of the loop gain: Integrator (\(z = 1\)): infinite gain at DC, zero steady-state error at the sample. Two zeros near or below the LC resonance: each gives back up to \(+90^\circ\). Below the resonance, they already give almost all their lead when the plant's phase plunges. Lower zeros give more phase at \(f_c\), but they lower the gain between the integrator and the resonance, and the loop becomes slow to correct errors in that band. High-frequency pole: limits the gain above the crossover, where there is only ripple and quantization noise (ADC quantization). When the ESR zero falls inside the band, the pole is placed on it to cancel it (The ESR zero). Gain \(K\): chosen last, so that \(|T| = 1\) at \(f_c\). The zeros and the pole go to \(z\) by matching (The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping): \(z_i = e^{-2\pi f_{zi}T_s}\) and \(p = e^{-2\pi f_p T_s}\), with the frequencies in hertz. Expanding the numerator and the denominator, \[C(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}},\] the firmware receives \(b_0 = K\), \(b_1 = -K(z_1+z_2)\), \(b_2 = K z_1 z_2\), \(a_1 = -(1+p)\) and \(a_2 = p\), and runs the difference equation \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\] The figure draws the same equation as a signal-flow diagram, in direct form I. Each \(z^{-1}\) box delays the signal by one period; the input gains (\(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\)) and the output gains (\(-a_1\), \(-a_2\)) multiply the samples; the circle \(\Sigma\) adds the five terms, and the sum is \(u[k]\). Direct form I of the 2p2z: the input e[k] goes through two one-period delays (z⁻¹) and the output u[k] through two more; the gains b₀, b₁ and b₂ on the input and −a₁ and −a₂ on the output all feed the adder Σ, which gives u[k] This is the velocity form: the integrator lives in the two past \(u\) terms. Since the integrator at \(z = 1\) forces \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\), the equation can be rewritten as \(u[k] - u[k-1] = a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\): the firmware computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to the previous duty. The code is in The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt; what happens when \(u\) saturates, in Anti-windup and duty saturation. title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: The relation with the PID
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In \(s\), the prototype is \[C(s) = K_I\,\frac{(1 + s/\omega_{z1})(1 + s/\omega_{z2})}{s\,(1 + s/\omega_p)} = K_P + \frac{K_I}{s} + \frac{K_D\,s}{1 + s\,T_F},\] a PID with a filter on the derivative. Matching coefficients, with \(\tau_{zi} = 1/(2\pi f_{zi})\) and \(\tau_f = 1/(2\pi f_p)\): \(K_P = K_I(\tau_{z1} + \tau_{z2} - \tau_f)\), \(K_D = K_I(\tau_{z1} - \tau_f)(\tau_{z2} - \tau_f)\) and \(T_F = \tau_f\). Both are the same linear controller. What changes is the way of designing (gains or roots) and the implementation: the PID keeps the integrator in a state of its own, which can be clamped; the velocity form has no such state. Design by roots, implement as you like Thinking in zeros, pole and crossover leads straight to the Bode plot. The PID gains come out afterwards, from the formulas above, if the firmware is a PID.

title: ADC quantization
heading: ADC quantization
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The digital controller doesn't see the output voltage: it sees an integer. In Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH), sampling made time discrete; here the A/D converter (ADC) makes the amplitude discrete, and everything the firmware knows about \(v_o\) goes through that rounding.

title: ADC quantization
heading: The step (LSB)
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: ADC step The step, or LSB (least significant bit), is the smallest change of the measured voltage that changes the code read. An \(N\)-bit ADC has \(2^N\) codes, from 0 to \(2^N - 1\): code 0 reads 0 V, the largest reads full scale, and between them the measuring range is divided into \(2^N - 1\) steps. The ADC pin only accepts 0 to \(V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) (3.3 V on an STM32). To measure a larger output, a resistive divider of ratio \(k_{\mathrm{div}}\) scales the voltage down, and the range referred to the output becomes \(V_{FS} = V_{\mathrm{ADC}}/k_{\mathrm{div}}\): \[q = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^{N} - 1} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{ADC}}}{(2^{N} - 1)\,k_{\mathrm{div}}}\] In the buck, \(V_{FS}\) = 20 V and \(N\) = 12 bits. The divider has \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = 3.3/20 = 0.165\), and \[q = \frac{20\ \text{V}}{4095} = 4.884\ \text{mV at the output} \qquad \left(\frac{3.3\ \text{V}}{4095} = 0.806\ \text{mV at the pin}\right).\] Code \(k\) reads \(k \cdot 20/4095\) V: the largest, 4095, reads exactly 20 V. That is the scale of the simulations' firmware (scenario.cpp), which rounds the sample to the nearest code. The range needs headroom above the nominal output, to see the overshoot and to protect against overvoltage, but every volt of headroom makes \(q\) coarser.

title: ADC quantization
heading: Quantization noise
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: When the voltage moves many steps between samples, the rounding error \(\varepsilon = v - q\cdot\text{code}\) spreads evenly between \(-q/2\) and \(q/2\). The variance of that uniform distribution is \[\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \frac{1}{q}\int_{-q/2}^{q/2} \varepsilon^2\, d\varepsilon = \frac{q^2}{12}, \qquad \sigma_\varepsilon = \frac{q}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.29\,q .\] In the buck, \(\sigma_\varepsilon = 4.884/\sqrt{12} = 1.41\) mV rms. This white-noise model holds during transients. In steady state it fails: the output barely changes, and the quantization error becomes a fixed error, or a repeating pattern. The same goes for a measurement: a signal that moves the sample by less than one code is lost in the rounding, which is why the sine that measures the loop gain grows with frequency (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty).

title: ADC quantization
heading: What the zero-error band means
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: For the controller, every output within a band of width \(q\) around the reference's code gives the same error. Inside that band the integrator has nothing to correct. The regulation's resolution is, at best, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 2.44\) mV at 9 V, or 0.03 %. That is resolution, not accuracy. The divider's tolerance and the ADC's gain and offset errors are worth tens of steps (see exercise 1). And the loop only settles inside the band if the duty has a level that puts the output there: if the digital PWM is coarser than the ADC, the output jumps over the band and the loop oscillates, which is the subject of DPWM resolution and limit cycles.

title: ADC quantization
heading: The reference as a code
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The firmware compares numbers. If the reference is written in volts, it almost never coincides with a code. With \(q = 20/4095\) V, 9 V is \(9 \cdot 4095/20 = 1842.75\) codes: the ADC only reads 1842 (8.9963 V) or 1843 (9.0012 V), and the error is \(+3.66\) mV or \(-1.22\) mV, never zero. The integrator goes up and down between the two codes forever. Write the reference as a code Compute the reference once, as an integer: REF_CODE = 1843, the code nearest to 1842.75. The loop then regulates at \(1843 \cdot 20/4095 = 9.0012\) V, 1.2 mV above 9 V, a quarter of a step. The error becomes REF_CODE - adc, an integer that can be exactly zero.

title: ADC quantization
heading: The sampling instant
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The output has switching ripple, and the loop regulates the sampled value, not the average: sampling always at the same phase of the period, the difference becomes a constant offset. The simulations sample at the start of each period, as in Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH). Sampling at the switching edge At the start of the period the high-side switch turns on, and on the board the measured voltage rings for tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, from the layout's parasitic inductances and the MOSFETs' capacitances. In the simulation the sample is clean; on the board, it is the worst instant. Trigger the ADC from the timer at a compare point away from the edges, for example in the middle of the on or off time, and check it on the scope. High-impedance divider The ADC's sampling capacitor charges through the divider during the sampling window. With resistors of hundreds of kΩ and a short window, it doesn't charge fully and the code comes out low. Use a capacitor at the pin, or a longer window. An RC filter at the pin also attenuates noise, but adds phase to the loop, like the delay of Computation and PWM delay.

title: ADC quantization
heading: In the converters
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Buck. \(q\) = 4.884 mV, against an output ripple of 17.6 mV peak to peak at 1 A (Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM): 3.6 steps. In the QSPICE scenarios, the output's average sits about 5 mV above the samples, because the sample falls near the ripple's valley (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). That is one ADC step of error, the same size as the zero-error band. Boost. The range is 60 V for a 48 V output, with 12 bits: \(q = 60/4095 = 14.65\) mV. The zero-error band, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 7.33\) mV, is 0.015 % of the output, half the buck's fraction. Buck-boost. 20 V and 12 bits, like the buck: \(q\) = 4.884 mV for a 12 V output. title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The averaged model describes the output's average over a period. The ADC does not read the average: it reads the voltage at one instant, and what that instant sees depends on the waveform. In the buck, the sample at the start of the period falls near the ripple's valley, a few millivolts below the average (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). In the boost and the buck-boost, the difference is larger and, besides, it changes with the duty and with the current: it becomes part of the plant.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: What the sample reads
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: This site's firmware triggers the ADC at the start of each period, just before G1 turns on. In the boost, G1 is the main switch: until then, G2 was conducting, and the capacitor received the inductor current minus the load's. Two effects add up: The capacitor ripple. While G1 conducts, only the capacitor feeds the load, and the voltage falls by \(\Delta v_C = I_o D T_s/C\); while G2 conducts, it rises again. The sample catches the end of the rise, the peak: \(\Delta v_C/2\) above the average. The ESR drop. On average, the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L - i_o = 0\). At the sampling instant, it receives \(i_L - i_o\): the whole inductor current, \(d\,i_L\) more than the average. The sample reads \(R_{ESR}\,d\,i_L\) more, minus the valley of the current ripple. The first effect is nearly constant and only shifts the regulated value: the loop regulates the sample, and the average sits below it. The second changes with \(d\) and with \(i_L\), and its linearization enters the plant: \[\hat v_s = \hat v + R_{ESR}\left(D\,\hat i_L + I\,\hat d\right)\] Plant seen by the ADC The transfer function from the duty to the sample, not to the average output. It is the one that enters the loop gain. In this site's boost and buck-boost, it is \(G_{vd}\) plus the ESR term, times the firmware's delay. The \(R_{ESR}\,I\,\hat d\) term does not fall with frequency. Well above the resonance, the \(-I(sL + R_l)\) term leaves the average output at about \(-I\,Z_o\,\hat d\), which includes \(-I\,R_{ESR}\,\hat d\); the sample cancels that part, and the right-half-plane zero moves up. The plant seen by the ADC gains a little phase near the crossover, and a design made with the average stays on the conservative side.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: The effective delay
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \((1 + D)\,T_s\) in the buck (Computation and PWM delay). In the boost and the buck-boost, the delay that best fits the QSPICE measurements, with the ESR term already in the model, is shorter: \[t_d = (1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s\] The 0.6 factor was found by fitting, comparing the model with the loop gain measured on the switched circuit (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty), not derived. The firmware's delay is still \((1 + D)\,T_s\); the smaller factor absorbs what the averaged model, even with the ESR term, does not yet describe, and should not be read as a physical delay. It holds for this firmware and this sampling instant. Phase margin of the boost's 2p2z at 1 A as a function of the delay: at 1.5 kHz, each period of delay costs only 5.4°.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: Why the instant matters
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The sampling instant decides three things: the offset between the regulated value and the average, the term added to the plant and the delay to the edge. Sampling in the middle of the interval in which G1 conducts, for example, catches the capacitor halfway down its fall, near the ripple's average, and the ESR with the constant current \(-i_o\), without the \(\hat i_L\) term, and the right-half-plane zero goes back to the average's. Compared with the sample at the edge, the 2p2z's margin loses about 2° to this term; the shorter delay gives part of it back, how much is not known without measuring the 0.6 factor again. In exchange, the ADC trigger has to follow the duty, with a second compare channel of the timer, and less time is left for the computation.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: In the converters
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Boost. At 1 A, the inductor current has a valley of 2.68 A, and at the sampling instant the ESR adds \(10\,\text{m}\Omega \times (2.68 - 1) = 17\) mV. The capacitor ripple is \(1\,\text{A} \times 0.752 \times 10\,\text{µs}/100\,\text{µF} = 75\) mV, and the peak sits 38 mV above the average. The sample should sit about 54 mV above the average. In QSPICE, with the samples regulated at 48.00 V, the output's average before the step is 47.95 V: Boost with the 2p2z, 1 A: before the step, the output's average is 47.95 V, about 50 mV below the regulated value. In the plant, the right-half-plane zero goes from 14.1 to 22.1 kHz at 1 A and from 6.9 to 8.4 kHz at 2 A. At the 2p2z's crossover, the ESR term adds 1.6° of margin: 45.3° instead of 43.7° at 1 A, and 40.6° instead of 39.0° at 2 A. The delay is \((1 + 0.6 \times 0.752) \times 10\,\text{µs} = 14.5\) µs, and it costs 7.8° at 1.5 kHz. With \((1 + D)\,T_s\), it would cost 1.6° more. With both terms, the model stayed within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, at 1 and 2 A. Buck-boost. At 12 V and 2 A, the capacitor ripple is \(2 \times 0.506 \times 10\,\text{µs}/100\,\text{µF} = 101\) mV, and the peak sits 51 mV above the average; the ESR adds another 7 mV. In the scenarios, the average before the reference step is 11.95 V. The ESR term takes the zero from 20.9 to 28.9 kHz and adds 1.1° of margin to the 2p2z. title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: Anti-windup and duty saturation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The duty has limits, and the linear 2p2z compensator doesn't know it. This note shows, step by step, how to keep an integrator from accumulating error while the output is saturated.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 1. Saturate the duty
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Every controller ends with a clamp to \([d_{\min}, d_{\max}]\). In the buck, \(d_{\min}\) = 0 and \(d_{\max}\) = 0.9. Besides the physical limit between 0 and 1, a maximum below 1 leaves time for the driver's bootstrap capacitor to recharge and an off interval to measure current. With \(d_{\max} = 0.9\), the buck only delivers 15 V if the input is above about 17 V.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 2. Understand windup
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: While the output is saturated, the loop is open: raising the command changes nothing. The integrator keeps adding the error, and that excess must be discharged later, with an error of the opposite sign, that is, with overshoot. The PID of scenario.cpp and buck_pid.cpp uses the simplest solution, the integrator clamp: the state is limited to the same range as the duty. integ += KI * T * err; if (integ < DMIN) integ = DMIN; /* anti-windup by clamping */ if (integ > DMAX) integ = DMAX; d = KP * err + integ + deriv; if (d < DMIN) d = DMIN; if (d > DMAX) d = DMAX; The clamp prevents the worst, but the integrator can still sit at \(d_{\max}\) when the operating point needs much less, and the output overshoots the reference while it unwinds. The example at the end of section 3 measures that overshoot in the boost.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 3. Or use the velocity form
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The 2p2z in C computes each duty from the two previous ones (equation Difference equation of the 2p2z) and stores the saturated ones. No state grows past the limits: the form is anti-windup by construction. It has one flaw, though. When a jump in the error saturates the duty, the next period's term \(b_1\,e[k-1]\) takes back the whole kick, which was never applied, and the duty plunges the other way. Measured in the boost: clamp versus velocity form QSPICE simulations of the boost, with the netlist and firmware of the scenarios. The same PID (\(K_P\) = 0.0114, \(K_I\) = 18.2, \(K_D\) = 1.75 µs/V, \(T_F\) = 7.96 µs) runs with the integrator clamp and as a 2p2z in velocity form, with the same transfer function. Settling, here, means entering the ±2 % band around 48 V for good. Input dropout. At 6 V, not even \(d_{\max} = 0.85\) is enough: the output stalls at 36.6 V, and the integrator sits on the clamp at 0.85, while the operating point at 12 V needs 0.76. The input then returns to 12 V at 10 V/ms. PID with clamp: another 450 µs at the limit, 33.8 A in the inductor, a 56.0 V peak, and settling in 1.79 ms. That is windup. Velocity form: 240 µs at the limit, 21.5 A, a 50.4 V peak, and settling in 0.96 ms. Reference step from 40 to 48 V, without slew. The derivative kick takes the duty to 0.85. PID with clamp: four periods at 0.85, no overshoot, and settling in 1.0 ms. Velocity form: this is the flaw above. The duty drops to 0.09 and stays at zero for two periods, the inductor current goes to −34.7 A, and the output plunges to 7.7 V. Even 3.6 ms after the step, it is at 46.6 V. The input dropout is not among the site's scenarios; the reference step is, with both controllers: Boost, reference step from 40 to 48 V without slew, PID with the integrator clamp: four periods at 0.85 and settling in 1.0 ms. The same step with the PID as a 2p2z in velocity form: the inductor current goes to −34.7 A and the output to 7.7 V.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 4. Back-calculation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: An alternative to the clamp is to feed back to the integrator the difference between the saturated and the computed command, with a time constant \(T_t\): \[x_I[k+1] = x_I[k] + K_I\,T_s\,e[k] + \frac{T_s}{T_t}\,\bigl(d_{\mathrm{sat}}[k] - d[k]\bigr).\] Outside saturation, the new term is zero. In saturation, it pulls the integrator to the value that keeps the command at the limit. A rule of thumb is \(T_t = \sqrt{T_i\,T_d}\), with \(T_i = K_P/K_I\) and \(T_d = K_D/K_P\).

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 5. Prevent it: reference slew and derivative on the measurement
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The best saturation is the one that doesn't happen. With a slew on the reference (soft-start), the error stays small during the transition. At 50 V/ms, the reference moves \(50\ \text{V/ms} \times 5\ \text{µs} = 0.25\) V per period. The derivative kick is the other trigger. On a reference step, \(e\) jumps, and \(K_D\,\Delta e/T_s\) jumps with it. Differentiating the measurement instead of the error removes the kick, because the reference leaves the derivative term: /* PID with back-calculation and derivative on the measurement */ float pid_step(float vref, float vmeas) { float e = vref - vmeas; float deriv = -KD * (vmeas - vmeas_prev) / T; /* no kick when vref changes */ float d = KP * e + integ + deriv; float dsat = d < DMIN ? DMIN : d > DMAX ? DMAX : d; integ += KI * T * e + (T / TT) * (dsat - d); /* back-calculation */ vmeas_prev = vmeas; return dsat; }

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: In the converters
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Buck. In the pid-vref-step scenario, the reference goes from 9 to 5 V without slew. The error jumps to −4 V, and the derivative term is \(K_D\,\Delta e/T_s = (1.5\ \mu/5\ \mu)\times(-4) = -1.2\). Added to \(K_P\,e = -0.23\) and to the integrator near 0.375, the command goes negative, and the duty is clamped to zero for one period. The low-side switch stays on for the whole period, and the inductor current goes negative, down to about −5 A: the high-side switch returns energy to the input. The duty then climbs back over about ten periods, and the output sinks to 4.30 V. With the 50 V/ms slew (scenario pid-vref), nothing saturates: the current stops at −2.5 A, and the output falls at most 35 mV below 5 V. Buck, reference step from 9 to 5 V without slew: the derivative kick sets the duty to zero for one period, and the inductor current goes to about −5 A. Buck, the same descent from 9 to 5 V with the 50 V/ms slew: no saturation, and the inductor current stops at −2.5 A. Boost. The boost's PID has a derivative filter, and the first period's kick is \(K_D/(T_F + T_s) = 0.097\) per volt of jump in the error. On the step from 48 to 40 V, that gives \(-0.78\), plus \(K_P\,e = -0.09\): the duty also goes to zero for one period, and the inductor current reaches −16 A. For about 0.25 ms, the synchronous rectifier carries it from the output back to the input. The boost's scenarios are gathered in Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example. Boost, reference step from 48 to 40 V without slew: one period at zero duty, and the inductor current reaches −16 A. Buck-boost. On the step from 12 to 8 V, the duty drops to 0.08 for one period, and the current reaches −4 A (Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example). Buck-boost, reference step from 12 to 8 V without a slew: the duty drops to 0.08 for one period, and the inductor current reverses down to −4 A. Exercise 2 With the 50 V/ms slew, how long does the descent from 9 to 5 V take in the buck, and what is the PID's derivative term (differentiating the error) in the ramp's first period? title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: Computation and PWM delay
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In an analog loop, a change at the output reaches the PWM comparator almost at once. In a digital one, the information travels a chain: the ADC converts, the interrupt computes, the PWM register is updated and, only then, an edge of the pulse moves. Each stage delays the response, and a pure delay \(t_d\) is \(e^{-s t_d}\): it leaves the magnitude of the loop gain alone, but takes phase.

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: The chain in this site's firmware
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Period \(k\) starts at \(t = kT_s\): Sample and conversion. The timer triggers the ADC at \(kT_s\) (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). The conversion takes from hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds. Computation. The end-of-conversion interrupt runs the PID or the 2p2z and writes the new duty to the compare register (CCR). Update in the next period. With preload on, the new CCR only takes effect at the next update event, at \((k+1)T_s\). This guarantees a whole pulse with the old value, even if the computation runs late, and costs one period. The modulated edge. In a trailing-edge (sawtooth) PWM, the switch turns on at the start of the period and off at \((k+1+D)T_s\). Only that edge depends on \(d\); the duty perturbation enters the plant there, \(DT_s\) after the start. Adding up, the delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\] The \(DT_s\) term plays the role of the zero-order hold: instead of the ZOH's average half period, the modulator delays up to the edge that actually moves. The PWM modulator also has a gain: in a real timer, \(d = \mathrm{CCR}/\mathrm{ARR}\), and an 850-step counter (170 MHz for 200 kHz) gives \(1/850\) per step. In this firmware the duty is computed per unit, as in Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins; and \(G_{vd}\) already includes \(V_{in}\). The resolution of those steps is the subject of DPWM resolution and limit cycles. For those coming from the reference course There, the digital loop's delay is "ZOH, \(-\omega T_s/2\), plus \(z^{-1}\) when the update goes to the next cycle", and no "PWM delay" is added to the ZOH. The rule is the same as here, written another way: that ZOH is the modulator, the time from the instant the new duty takes effect to the edge it moves (or to the midpoint of the two edges, when both move). In that course's symmetric PWM, with the update at the triangle's peak or valley, that midpoint lies half a period after the update for any \(D\), and the modulator is worth \(T_s/2\). In this site's trailing-edge PWM, only the falling edge moves, \(DT_s\) after the start of the period. Hence \[(1+D)\,T_s = \underbrace{T_s}_{z^{-1}} + \underbrace{T_s/2}_{\text{ZOH}} + \underbrace{(D-\tfrac12)\,T_s}_{\text{edge position}}.\] With \(D = 0.5\), both counts give \(1.5\,T_s\). In the buck, with \(D = 0.375\), "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" counts \(1.5\,T_s\) instead of \(1.375\,T_s\): \(1.8^\circ\) more phase at 8 kHz, and the 2p2z's margin comes out \(39.6^\circ\) instead of \(41.3^\circ\). The error is small and on the safe side because \(D < 0.5\); with \(D > 0.5\) it would be optimistic. Do not add the ZOH's phase to \((1+D)\,T_s\): it is already inside the \(DT_s\) term. The note PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric shows, in a timing diagram, when each PWM loads the new duty and which edges move, and compares the timings. Phase of the buck's loop gain near the crossover, and the phase margin against the delay, from 0 to 2Tₛ: each period of delay costs 360°·fc·Tₛ /* ADC end-of-conversion interrupt, triggered by the timer at t = kTs. */ void ADC_IRQHandler(void) { float v = adc_read() * (VFS / 4095.0f); /* sample at kTs, in volts */ float d = control_step(vref - v); /* PID or 2p2z */ TIM1->CCR1 = (uint32_t)(d * ARR); /* preload: takes effect at (k + 1)Ts */ }

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: Other timings
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Update in the same period. Without preload, if the new CCR is written before the falling edge of the current pulse, the delay drops to \(DT_s\). The computation must fit in \(DT_s\): in the buck, \(0.375 \times 5\ \text{µs} = 1.9\ \text{µs}\), conversion included. Center-aligned PWM. The counter counts up and down, and the pulse is centered on the valley. With the sample at the valley and the load at the peak, the effective delay, from the sample to the center of the pulse it governs, is exactly \(T_s\), for any \(D\); both edges move, and the sample at the center of the pulse is far from them. Computation that misses its deadline. If the interrupt ends after the update event, the value only takes effect one period later: \((2+D)T_s\). Jitter and priorities The delay is only \((1+D)T_s\) if the control interrupt never misses its deadline. A higher-priority communication interrupt, a slow flash access or a debug printf can push the CCR write past the update event in some periods, and the loop then has a varying delay. Give the control the highest priority, and time the routine with an output pin and the oscilloscope. Phase budget Before choosing \(f_c\), compute the phase the delay will take. If it is more than about 30°, the crossover is too high for the chosen timing.

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: In the converters
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the buck, with \(D = 0.375\) and \(T_s = 5\ \text{µs}\) (200 kHz), \(t_d = 6.875\ \text{µs}\). At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the delay takes \(19.8^\circ\): \(14.4^\circ\) from the computation period and \(5.4^\circ\) from the \(DT_s\) term. At 18 kHz, \(44.6^\circ\); at 25 kHz, \(61.9^\circ\). It is the main reason why the aggressive and unstable designs lose their margin. The model with \((1+D)T_s\) was checked in QSPICE by adding a small sine to the duty inside the firmware: from 500 Hz to 15 kHz, it was within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of the simulation (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). In the boost and the buck-boost, the delay that best fits the QSPICE measurements is \((1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s\), found by fitting rather than derived, with the sample's ESR term already in the model (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). With the boost's crossover at 1.5 kHz, it matters little; the limit there is the The right-half-plane zero. title: Discretization table
heading: Discretization table
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behaviour and when to use each.
text: A controller designed in \(s\) has to become a difference equation. The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping introduced the bilinear transform, and Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) introduced the zero-order hold. This table gathers those two and the other common methods, with \(T_s = 1/f_s\) the sampling period.

title: Discretization table
heading: The maps
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behaviour and when to use each.
text: Method Substitution or rule The left half of the \(s\) plane goes to DC gain High frequency When to use Forward Euler \(s \to \dfrac{z - 1}{T_s}\) the half plane \(\mathrm{Re}\,z < 1\): a stable pole can leave the unit circle kept (\(s = 0 \to z = 1\)) the axis \(s = j2\pi f\) becomes the line \(z = 1 + j2\pi f\,T_s\), outside the circle; the error grows with \(2\pi f\,T_s\) almost never in a compensator; only for dynamics very slow compared with \(f_s\) Backward Euler \(s \to \dfrac{1 - z^{-1}}{T_s}\) the disk of radius 1/2 centered at \(z = 1/2\): always stable, but too damped kept \(s \to \infty\) goes to \(z = 0\) a PID's integrator and derivative; simple filters Tustin (bilinear) \(s \to \dfrac{2}{T_s}\,\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}\) exactly the unit disk kept \(f \to \infty\) goes to \(z = -1\) (\(f_s/2\)); frequencies are compressed, \(f_d = \tfrac{1}{\pi T_s}\arctan(\pi f_a T_s)\) the default for compensators Prewarped Tustin \(s \to \dfrac{2\pi f_0}{\tan(\pi f_0 T_s)}\,\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}\) the unit disk kept like Tustin, but exact at \(f_0\) when one frequency must land in place: the crossover, a notch ZOH equivalent \(G(z) = (1 - z^{-1})\,\mathcal{Z}\{G(s)/s\}\) exact poles, \(z = e^{pT_s}\) kept exact for a staircase input; a strictly proper \(G\) ends up with \(b_0 = 0\), which adds one period of delay discretizing the plant seen by the PWM, not the compensator Matched pole-zero each pole and zero goes to \(z = e^{pT_s}\); zeros at infinity go to \(z = -1\); the gain is matched at DC or another frequency the unit disk (exact poles) matched the finite zeros are exact too; the phase of fast poles differs from the continuous one poles and zeros with a physical meaning, as in this course's 2p2z The methods agree when the singularity is slow compared with \(f_s\) and diverge as it approaches \(f_s/2\). The figure shows it on the buck's 2p2z. The buck's default 2p2z (zeros at 2 kHz, pole at 60 kHz, crossover at 8 kHz) discretized at 200 kHz: compare the discrete response with the continuous one near the fast pole.

title: Discretization table
heading: Reading the table
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behaviour and when to use each.
text: Stability: only forward Euler can make a stable pole unstable. A real pole at \(s = -2\pi f_p\) goes to \(z = 1 - 2\pi f_p T_s\), which leaves the circle when \(f_p > f_s/\pi\). DC gain: all of them keep the gain at \(z = 1\), which is why the integrator stays an integrator. Matched pole-zero keeps it because the gain is chosen to. Delay: the ZOH equivalent of a compensator without a direct term adds one period of delay. That is why it serves for the plant, in Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH), and not for the controller. Frequency warping: in Tustin, it is negligible below \(f_s/10\) and large near \(f_s/2\). Prewarping fixes one frequency only (see The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping).

title: Discretization table
heading: In the converters
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behaviour and when to use each.
text: Buck. The default design at 200 kHz has zeros at 2 kHz and a pole at 60 kHz, and scenarios.json takes it to \(z\) by matched pole-zero: the pole goes to \(p = e^{-2\pi \cdot 60\,\text{k}\cdot T_s} = 0.1518\), which is \(a_2\), and \(a_1 = -(1 + p) = -1.1518\). The four substitution methods give, for the two singularities: Method zero at 2 kHz pole at 60 kHz Forward Euler 0.93717 −0.8850 Backward Euler 0.94088 0.3466 Tustin 0.93908 0.0296 matched 0.93910 0.1518 At the zero, at 1 % of \(f_s\), the four agree to two decimal places. The pole, at 30 % of \(f_s\), lands in four different places: forward Euler puts it near \(z = -1\), ringing at \(f_s/2\), and Tustin turns it into a pole that, seen in frequency, sits at 48.1 kHz instead of 60 kHz. The PID of scenario.cpp uses backward Euler: integ += KI * T * err adds the current error, and the derivative is \(K_D\,(e[k] - e[k-1])/T_s\), with its filter also discretized by backward Euler. Exercise 1 In the buck, above what frequency does a real pole of the compensator discretized by forward Euler become unstable? Exercise 2 By Tustin without prewarping, at what frequency does the 60 kHz pole appear? What constant replaces \(2/T_s\) so that it lands exactly at 60 kHz? title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In ADC quantization, the measurement of the output moved in steps. So does the actuator: the digital PWM (DPWM) only produces a finite number of duty values, and the two quantizers together can keep the loop from settling.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: The DPWM step
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: A timer counts clock pulses from 0 to the end of the period, and the PWM output changes when the counter passes the compare value (the CCR register). The duty can only be \(\mathrm{CCR}/N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\): \[N_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{f_s}, \qquad \Delta D = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{PWM}}}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \log_2 N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\] On an STM32G4 with the timer at 170 MHz and \(f_s\) = 200 kHz, there are \(170/0.2 = 850\) counts per period: \(\Delta D = 1/850\), or \(\log_2 850 = 9.7\) bits. In center-aligned mode (the counter goes up and down) 425 counts remain, 8.7 bits. The resolution gets worse with the switching frequency: doubling \(f_s\) costs one bit. High-resolution timers solve this. The STM32G4's HRTIM divides each 170 MHz cycle into 32 (184 ps steps), which is like counting at 5.44 GHz: 27,200 counts at 200 kHz, or 14.7 bits. Other manufacturers have similar peripherals.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: The step at the output
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In steady state, changing the duty by \(\Delta D\) moves the output by \(|G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D\), with \(G_{vd}\) the plant of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) \approx V_{in}\): \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = \frac{24\ \text{V}}{850} = 28.2\ \text{mV} \qquad \text{against} \qquad q = 4.884\ \text{mV}.\] One step of the ordinary timer moves the output almost six ADC steps. No CCR value puts the output inside the ADC's zero-error band, which is only 4.884 mV wide. The buck's two quantizers: a 12-bit ADC and a 10-bit DPWM (1024 counts, 23.4 mV per step at the output). Change the resolutions and see when a DPWM level appears inside the zero-error band.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: Limit cycle
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Limit cycle A sustained periodic oscillation of a nonlinear system, with no external excitation. In a quantized loop, the output alternates between DPWM levels because none of them cancels the error read. The mechanism is simple. The integrator accumulates the error and raises the duty one step; the output rises 28 mV and jumps over the band; the error changes sign, the integrator goes down, and the story repeats. The linear analysis of Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins doesn't predict it: the loop can have good margins and still oscillate, with an amplitude of the order of the DPWM step. Peterchev and Sanders (2003) gave three conditions for removing steady-state limit cycles: a DPWM finer than the ADC, so that a DPWM level exists inside the zero-error band. They suggest one extra bit, which gives two DPWM levels per ADC level; an integrator in the controller, with limited gain. Without it, an error remains in steady state and the resting point doesn't fall inside the band; with too much gain, it can't adjust the duty in fine steps. With the variables normalized to \(V_{in}\), the integral gain lies between 0 and 1; no excess loop gain: the ADC acts as a gain that changes with the signal's amplitude (its describing function), and the loop, with that gain, must not pass through the −1 point. In practice, this asks for headroom in the gain margin. The first two, the static conditions, read: \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = |G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D < q, \qquad 0 < k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)| \le 1\] They assume that the zero-error band exists: with the reference between two codes, as in ADC quantization, the integrator hunts forever.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: Dither
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: When resolution is short, the firmware can alternate the CCR between two neighboring values over \(M\) periods. The LC filter takes the average, and the average duty moves in steps of \(\Delta D/M\). The price is a component at the frequency \(f_s/M\), which must fall well above the crossover and be attenuated by the LC. /* Dither over M = 8 periods. d8 is the duty in counts with 3 fraction bits (d * 850 * 8). The bit-reversed order spreads the "high" periods. */ static const uint8_t threshold[8] = {0, 4, 2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 7}; static uint32_t k; uint32_t ccr_with_dither(uint32_t d8) { uint32_t base = d8 >> 3, frac = d8 & 7u; return base + (frac > threshold[k++ & 7u]); /* frac periods out of 8 get +1 */ } The integrator also needs resolution With \(k_i\,q/\Delta D \ll 1\), each sample moves the integrator by a fraction of a count. If the state is stored in whole counts, the increment rounds to zero and the integrator never moves: an artificial dead band. Store the state with fraction bits, as in Q15 fixed point.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: In the converters
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Buck. This site's simulations quantize only the ADC: the duty is a double, and the PWM edges fall at the exact instant. Condition 1 holds by construction, and the scenarios show no DPWM limit cycles. On an STM32G4 it would be different: 28.2 mV with the ordinary timer breaks the condition, and 0.88 mV with the HRTIM meets it. Condition 2 holds with room to spare. In the PID, \(k_i = K_I T_s\) = 1309 × 5 µs = 0.0065 per volt, and \(k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)| = 0.0065 \times 24 = 0.16\). In the 2p2z, the integrator moves \((b_0 + b_1 + b_2)/(1 - a_2) = 1.01\times10^{-3}\) per volt and per sample, and the product is 0.024. With the 170 MHz timer, that integrator would move only \(k_i\,q/\Delta D = 0.0042\) of a count per code of error, and would need the resolution of the warning above. Boost. The static gain is much larger: \(V_{in}/(1-D)^2 \approx 12/0.248^2 \approx 195\) V per unit of duty, at 48 V and 1 A. At 100 kHz, the 170 MHz timer makes 1700 counts, and each moves the output 0.11 V, against \(q\) = 14.65 mV. Even the HRTIM gives 3.6 mV per step, below \(q\), but with less room. Exercise 2 With the 170 MHz timer at 200 kHz, what \(M\) (a power of 2) does the dither need to meet condition 1 in the buck? title: Q15 fixed point
heading: Q15 fixed point
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The 2p2z compensator has coefficients such as 0.23114 and −0.43413. With a floating-point unit, they go into the code as they are. Without one, each number becomes an integer with an implicit scale.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: Float or fixed point?
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: With an FPU (Cortex-M4F, M7, M33 with FPU, such as the STM32G4, F4 and H7): use float. The single-precision FPU multiplies and adds in one to three cycles (typical datasheet figures, not measured here), and the 24-bit mantissa is more than enough for this loop. Without an FPU (Cortex-M0 and M0+, such as the STM32G0 and C0): every float operation becomes a library call of, typically, tens of cycles. With a 5 µs period and a 64 MHz core, there are only 320 cycles per period. Here fixed point is used. Hidden double precision On a single-precision FPU, 0.5 is a double, and x * 0.5 is computed in software. Write 0.5f, and compile with -Wdouble-promotion so the compiler points out the cases.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: The Qm.n format
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Qm.n format A signed integer \(X\) represents \(x = X/2^n\): \(n\) fraction bits and \(m\) integer bits besides the sign, \(1 + m + n\) bits in all. Q15 (or Q0.15) is the int16_t read as a fraction, from −1 to \(1 - 2^{-15}\), in steps of \(3.05\times10^{-5}\). \[x = \frac{X}{2^{n}}, \quad X \in \left[-2^{m+n},\; 2^{m+n}-1\right], \qquad Z = \left\lfloor \frac{X\,Y + 2^{n-1}}{2^{n}} \right\rfloor\] Q2.13 covers −4 to 4 in steps of \(1.22\times10^{-4}\): it trades resolution for headroom. The product of two Q15 numbers has 30 fraction bits and fits in 32 bits. To return to Q15, add half a step (\(2^{14}\)) and shift by 15 bits: #include <stdint.h> static inline int16_t sat16(int32_t x) /* saturate instead of wrapping */ { return x > INT16_MAX ? INT16_MAX : x < INT16_MIN ? INT16_MIN : (int16_t)x; } static inline int16_t q15_mul(int16_t a, int16_t b) { int32_t p = (int32_t)a * b; /* Q30: the cast comes before the multiplication */ p += 1 << 14; /* round instead of truncating */ return sat16(p >> 15); /* -1 * -1 = +1 doesn't fit in Q15: saturate */ } Three pitfalls Overflow: without saturation, \(0.9 + 0.2\) in Q15 becomes \(-0.9\). A duty that jumps from 0.9 to −0.9 is the worst possible error. On the Cortex-M3 and M4, CMSIS offers __SSAT(x, 16), which saturates in one instruction. Truncation: p >> 15 without the half step always rounds down, a bias that the integrator accumulates. Shifting negatives: in C99, >> of a negative number is implementation-defined. In GCC for ARM it is arithmetic; check your compiler. To add several products, use a 64-bit accumulator. Each Q15 × Q15 product already takes 31 bits, and two of them added can overflow 32 bits. On the Cortex-M4, the SMLAL instruction multiplies and accumulates in 64 bits in one cycle, according to the core's manual. The M0 has no such instruction, and the compiler emulates the operation with several.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: The buck's 2p2z coefficients
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The default design (crossover at 8 kHz, double zeros at 2 kHz, pole at 60 kHz) has, in duty per volt of error, \(b_0 = 0.23114\), \(b_1 = -0.43413\), \(b_2 = 0.20385\) and, in the denominator, \(a_1 = -(1 + p) = -1.15184\) and \(a_2 = p = 0.15184\). The \(a_i\) relate \(u\) to \(u\) and don't depend on the units. In the difference equation, \(a_1\) exceeds 1 in magnitude and doesn't fit in Q15. There are two ways out: Velocity form: rewrite the equation as \(u[k-1] + a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + \dots\), so that only \(a_2\) has to be stored, in Q15: 4975. \(a_1\) stays implicit, \(-(2^{15} + 4975)/2^{15}\), and exact. A format with headroom for both: in Q1.14, which goes from −2 to almost 2, \(a_1\) = −18872 and \(a_2\) = 2488. Either way, \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) share one format. Since \(2^n\) is an integer, rounding both at the same scale keeps \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\) exact, and the integrator stays at \(z = 1\). With \(a_1\) in Q1.14 and \(a_2\) in Q15, the sum would be \(-3.05\times10^{-5}\), and the integrator would move to \(z = 1.000036\), outside the unit circle. Units matter too. The firmware receives ADC codes and writes counts to the CCR. Multiplying the coefficients by \(N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\,q = 850 \times 4.884\ \text{mV} = 4.15\), they become counts per code: \(0.960\), \(-1.802\) and \(0.846\). Now \(b_1\) exceeds 1, and the format needs headroom: Q1.14 is enough, and Q2.13 accepts larger designs. The script below quantizes the coefficients and measures the effect: import numpy as np fs, q, N = 200e3, 20/4095, 850 b = np.array([0.23114164, -0.43413087, 0.20384645]); p = 0.15183580 a1, a2 = -(1 + p), p # denominator 1 + a1 z^-1 + a2 z^-2 K = N * q # from duty/volt to counts/code ki = b.sum() / (1 - a2) # integrator step per sample for n in (15, 14): # a1 and a2 at the same scale: 1 + a1 + a2 = 0 exactly A1, A2 = round(a1 * 2**n), round(a2 * 2**n) print(f"a in Q{15 - n}.{n}", A1, A2, 2**n + A1 + A2) # Q0.15: -37743 does not fit in int16 for name, n, scale in [("Q15 d/V", 15, 1), ("Q2.13 d/V", 13, 1), ("Q4.11 d/V", 11, 1), ("Q2.13 cnt/code", 13, K), ("Q1.14 cnt/code", 14, K)]: B = np.round(b * scale * 2**n) # the integers stored in the firmware bq = B / 2**n / scale a2q = np.round(a2 * 2**15) / 2**15 # a2 in Q15: 4975; a1 = -(1 + a2) implicit f = np.abs(np.log(np.roots(bq))) * fs / (2 * np.pi) print(name, B.astype(int), np.round(f), f"{100 * (bq.sum() / (1 - a2q) / ki - 1):+.1f} %") Format, units \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\) zeros (were double at 2 kHz) integral gain phase margin exact — 2000 and 2000 Hz — 41.3° Q15, duty/V 7574, −14226, 6680 1904 and 2094 Hz −0.3 % 41.3° Q2.13, duty/V 1894, −3556, 1670 complex pair, 2135 Hz +13.9 % 41.1° Q4.11, duty/V 473, −889, 417 686 and 3325 Hz −43 % 41.7° Q2.13, counts/code 7861, −14764, 6932 1836 and 2167 Hz −0.5 % 41.3° Q1.14, counts/code 15721, −29528, 13865 1863 and 2136 Hz −0.5 % 41.3° The pole, with \(a_2\) = 4975 in Q15, moves from 60,000 to 60,002 Hz; with \(a_2\) = 2488 in Q1.14, to 59,996 Hz. The margins come from the buck's model in tools/qspice_loop_check.py. The table has two lessons: The margin barely changes. Near the crossover, an error of \(10^{-4}\) in a coefficient of 0.4 is negligible. The integrator and the double zero change a lot. The integral gain is proportional to \(b_0 + b_1 + b_2 = 8.6\times10^{-4}\), a sum 270 times smaller than \(b_0\), made of nearly equal numbers that cancel. A double zero is ill-conditioned: an error \(\delta\) in the coefficients splits it by about \(\sqrt{\delta}\). That is why scaling matters: in Q2.13, the coefficients in counts per code use four times more of the range than in duty per volt, and the integral gain's error falls from 13.9 % to 0.5 %.
